articles.title: CELEBRATING 100 YEARS

paras.en: MEDINA, OH (January 6, 2025) – Carlisle Brake & Friction (CarlisleCBF), a global leader in brake and friction technology and part of the CentroMotion family of brands, has reached a momentous milestone – its 100th anniversary.
Since its founding in 1925, the company has lived up to its tagline, "Braking New Ground," by consistently pioneering innovative solutions that have propelled industries forward.

"For 100 years, Carlisle has been synonymous with groundbreaking innovation and unwavering reliability in the braking industry," says Tom Vanderlaan, Chief Commercial Officer (CCO) of CentroMotion. "This milestone is a testament to the dedication of our employees, the trust of our customers, and the enduring strength of our products. As we celebrate our centennial, we reaffirm our commitment to continuous innovation, strong partnerships, and giving back to the communities we serve."
A Century of Innovation in Motion Control

For a century, CarlisleCBF has been at the forefront of motion control, pushing the boundaries of performance with its industry-leading brakes and friction materials. Through unwavering commitment to R&D, the company has earned the trust of customers worldwide, establishing itself as a cornerstone of reliability.
Celebrating 100 Years of Braking New Ground: A Digital Celebration

To commemorate this historic milestone, CarlisleCBF is launching a comprehensive digital celebration. This virtual experience will allow customers, employees and industry partners to delve into the company’s rich history, groundbreaking innovations and commitment to excellence through historical photographs and stories.

A core aspect of the celebration is fostering a sense of community. CarlisleCBF invites customers, employees and industry partners to join the journey by visiting their dedicated anniversary webpage, www.CarlisleCBF.com, and following their story on social media.
The webpage and social media channels will serve as a virtual time capsule, showcasing CarlisleCBF's rich history, ground-breaking milestones and product innovations.

To encourage participation and celebrate the impact CarlisleCBF has had, a social media campaign is launching with the hashtag #CarlisleCBF100. Participants are encouraged to share stories, photos and memories that illustrate how CarlisleCBF products have impacted their lives or businesses. The most engaging submissions will be featured on the company's social media channels and website.
By combining digital storytelling with interactive social media, CarlisleCBF aims to create a lasting legacy for its first century of service, while fostering a spirit of community and appreciation.

Carlisle Brake & Friction, a CentroMotion brand, is a globally recognized leader in the development and manufacture of highly innovative brake and friction system solutions to service a diverse range of motion control applications. The comprehensive nature of CarlisleCBF's brake system expertise includes hydraulic control products, industrial brake assemblies, and wet and dry friction material for brake, clutch, and transmission applications, as well as aftermarket replacement products. Our full-system product offering, supported by our industry-experience staff of experts, provides our customers with brake system solutions that set them apart from their competition. www.carlislecbf.com

articles.title: Texas Finalizes Landmark Mandatory Right to Appraisal Rules
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: A ten-year campaign to address insurance under-indemnification in Texas has culminated in the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI) adopting rules implementing Senate Bill 458 under Texas Administrative Code, Title 28, Part 1, Chapter 5, Subchapter Q, Division 4 (§§5.9800-5.9806).

The rules establish the Mandatory Right to Appraisal (RTA) framework for personal automobile and residential property insurance claims. They set standardized procedures, timelines, minimum qualifications for appraisal participants and consumer notification requirements. The framework is intended to provide a structured process for resolving disputes over the amount of loss and strengthen policyholders’ ability to challenge claim settlements without litigation.

“This is one of the most significant shifts in Texas insurance regulation that I’ve seen over my career,” said Robert McDorman, president and founder of Auto Claim Specialists. “For too long, policyholders have faced an uphill battle when challenging inadequate claim settlements. These rules help level the playing field by establishing a clear, enforceable process that gives Texas consumers a meaningful opportunity to exercise the protections the Legislature intended.”
Revisions to Umpire Selection and Appraisal Deadlines

TDI revised §5.9806(b)(3) after public comments to ensure only the policyholder may invoke an independent-vendor umpire-selection option. Insurers may include such vendors in policies but cannot require policyholders to use that mechanism. The rules require insurers to include judicial appointment as an available option when appraisers cannot agree on an umpire.

TDI also changed the deadline for demanding appraisal in personal automobile claims. The original proposal generally required appraisal within 120 days after claim acceptance or rejection. Under adopted §5.9806(a), the deadline is tied to the policy’s limitations period for filing suit. The final rules set more restrictive deadlines once litigation has begun.

“The umpire rule needs to be crystal clear that judicial appointment must always remain an available option when appraisers cannot agree on an umpire,” McDorman said. “Most policyholders lack the resources or sophistication to challenge a carrier-embedded umpire-selection process, making it critical that insurers cannot force consumers into a mechanism they did not choose.”

The regulations set procedures for conducting appraisals, including deadlines for appointing appraisers, selecting umpires and reaching an award. For personal automobile claims, each party generally must appoint an appraiser within 20 days of a demand, and appraisers have 40 days to attempt agreement on the amount of loss. If an umpire is involved, an award must be issued within 180 days of the original demand, with the ability to modify deadlines by written agreement.
Insurers must notify policyholders of appraisal rights when issuing claim acceptance or rejection notices.

According to TDI’s “Appraisal Experience Data Call Report,” approximately 98% of personal automobile appraisals resulted in awards exceeding insurers’ initial offers. Research by Auto Claim Specialists found appraisal increased settlements by an average of $6,111 for repair claims and $4,044 for total losses.

“Every dollar represents a Texas family trying to restore their vehicle,” said McDorman. When people aren’t fully indemnified, they’re forced to pay out of pocket, delay necessary repairs or accept unsafe compromises. This has always been about protecting consumers.

“When insurers know there’s a fair, enforceable appraisal process available, they’re motivated to evaluate claims more accurately from the beginning. A credible dispute-resolution process benefits everyone by encouraging better claim practices across the board.”

The effort followed TDI’s 2015 approval of State Farm’s request to remove the Appraisal Clause from its Texas automobile policies for repair procedure disputes. McDorman, the Auto Body Association of Texas‘ Burl Richards and Texas Watch Executive Director Ware Wendell helped organize a sustained campaign to restore appraisal as a dispute-resolution mechanism. McDorman met with TDI officials and testified before legislative committees, and wrote a monthly “Ask the Expert” column in Texas Automotive.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This legislative effort was supported by Auto Claim Specialists’ lobbyist Andrew “Drew” Graham of Graham Public Affairs, alongside Jacob Smith and Jesus Moreno of Longleaf Consulting. S.B. 458 passed unanimously in 2025, authored by Sen. Charles Schwertner (R-District 5) and sponsored in the House by Rep. Jay Dean (R-District 7).

“The statute gave consumers the Right to Appraisal; the rules determine whether that right works effectively,” McDorman said. Recommendations during rulemaking addressed umpire independence, potential financial conflicts involving insurer-designated vendors, consumer costs, professional qualifications and regulatory enforcement.

“For years, our conversations focused on helping regulators understand the challenges Texas consumers were facing. Throughout this process, the department demonstrated a willingness to evaluate empirical data and consider recommendations from a broad range of stakeholders. They didn’t simply hold public hearings — they listened. When we presented evidence showing why judicial appointment needed to remain an available option if appraisers could not agree on an umpire, TDI considered those concerns and revised the final rule. That’s exactly how the regulatory process is supposed to work.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “This victory belongs to a tremendous number of people; it wasn’t the accomplishment of one organization or one individual. ABAT stood beside us from the beginning, Texas Watch consistently championed consumers and many collision repair professionals, attorneys, public adjusters and policyholders shared their experiences to help educate decision-makers. Legislators from both parties took the time to understand the issue instead of viewing it politically. We accomplished this together.

“This victory results from 10 years of consistent messaging. We didn’t change our message because the facts never changed. We simply continued presenting the evidence until everyone understood why this mattered.”

The new appraisal requirements apply to personal automobile and residential property insurance policies delivered, issued for delivery or renewed in Texas on or after March 1, 2027. The implementation period allows insurers to update policy language, obtain approvals and incorporate appraisal notices into claims procedures.

“Our work isn’t finished simply because the rules have been adopted,” said McDorman. “Now, we have the responsibility to ensure Texans understand they have this protection available. Rights only matter if people know they exist.

“We went up against incredible odds. The insurance industry possesses enormous financial resources, and for years, individual consumers simply didn’t have the same voice. But persistence and facts matter. When you’re willing to do the work, present credible evidence and keep fighting for the right reasons, meaningful change is possible.

“This was never about defeating the insurance industry. It was about protecting Texas families. Because lawmakers listened, because TDI remained open-minded throughout the process and because so many organizations and individuals refused to give up, Texas consumers won! These rules will help ensure fairer settlements, safer repairs and stronger consumer protections for generations to come. That will make a difference for real people, and that’s what makes all our hard work worthwhile.

“Other states are watching what happens here. Texas has demonstrated that protecting consumers and creating clear, consistent claim procedures are not mutually exclusive. In fact, they strengthen the insurance system by creating greater accountability, predictability and public confidence.”

With Division 4 adopted, the framework establishes procedures, minimum qualifications, consumer notifications and protections around selecting independent appraisal participants. As Texas approaches March 2027 implementation, the framework is presented as a more balanced insurance claims system for policyholders.

articles.title: Eddie Pettus Wins 2026 SEMA Battle of the Builders with 1970 Chevrolet Chevelle
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: Eddie Pettus won the overall title at the 2026 SEMA Battle of the Builders presented by Mothers competition with his 1970 Chevrolet Chevelle. After winning the Hot Rod/Hot Rod Truck category, Pettus advanced to the final round with fellow class champions Buddy Hale (Sport Compact/Import Performance), Mark Giambalvo (Off-Road) and Jesse Rieger (Young Guns).

“This is just awesome, and it was such a tough year,” said Pettus. “It means so much to me and my team to do this, and to finally get the overall is an honor. The Chevelle was a five-year build, over 15,000 man-hours between the interior and the car being built.”

The Chevelle is powered by a 1,300-horsepower twin-turbo LS3 engine paired with a 4L80 transmission from Bowler Performance. The drivetrain is supported by a Roadster Shop chassis with cantilever independent rear suspension and Brembo brakes, providing the foundation for the car’s performance.

The exterior features a wedge-sectioned body, extended wheelbase and modified roofline, along with custom rocker panels and fender extensions. Pettus also incorporated flush-mounted glass, custom floor pans, wheelwells and firewall. The build is finished with an Avante Garde-designed interior, Dakota Digital gauges and custom wheels, grille, bumpers, lighting and exhaust.

“Eddie’s Chevelle demonstrates the creativity, craftsmanship and technical expertise that define SEMA Battle of the Builders,” said RJ de Vera, vice president of marketing for SEMA. “The competition recognizes the talent, innovation and passion that drive the automotive and powersports industries. We’re proud to celebrate the builders who continue to push the boundaries of vehicle design and fabrication.”

The SEMA Battle of the Builders competition features four categories, with each category winner competing for the overall title. Hale won Sport Compact/Import Performance with a 1955 Volkswagen Ghia, while Giambalvo earned the Off-Road title with a 1974 Chevrolet K10. Rieger won the Young Guns category with a 1969 Ford Mustang.
For more information on the SEMA Battle of the Builders competition and this year’s winners, visit sema.org/botb.

articles.title: Boyd Group Reports 28% Revenue Growth Despite Continued Decline in Collision Claims
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: Boyd Group Services Inc. reported a 28.2% increase in third-quarter revenue to more than $1 billion, even as the collision repair industry continues to struggle with declining insurance claims volumes that have pressured repair facilities over the past two years.

The company’s financial results, released Nov. 11, highlight the contrasting fortunes of collision repair businesses operating in a challenging market. While many repairers continue to contend with fewer vehicles coming through their doors, Boyd has managed to increase revenue and profitability through acquisitions, market share gains and operational efficiencies.

Perhaps the most significant takeaway for the broader collision repair industry was Boyd’s assessment of repairable insurance claims volume. The company estimates that repairable claims declined approximately 1% to 3% year over year during the third quarter of 2026, indicating that the industry’s prolonged downturn has yet to reverse.
Boyd said the decline was consistent with its long-term planning assumptions, suggesting the company is not counting on a significant recovery in collision repair demand in the near term.

Despite those market conditions, Boyd reported third-quarter sales of $1.013 billion, compared to $790.2 million during the same period in 2025. Much of that growth came from acquisitions, including Joe Hudson’s Collision Center, with locations added since the comparable quarter contributing $206 million in revenue.

More importantly, Boyd achieved 2.2% same-store sales growth during the quarter, indicating that its existing operations generated additional revenue despite the overall decline in industry claims. The company attributed that performance to market share gains, strong insurer relationships and a modest increase in the total cost of repairs.

“Our third quarter results reflect continued progress on our strategic priorities and ongoing outperformance of broader industry trends,” said Brian Kaner, president and CEO of Boyd Group. “Revenue increased 28%, supported by the addition of Joe Hudson’s, market share gains and positive same-store sales growth.”

Boyd’s results illustrate an increasingly important distinction in the collision repair industry: Revenue growth at large multi-shop operators does not necessarily indicate that overall collision repair demand is recovering.

With repairable claims volume continuing to decline, collision repair businesses are competing for a smaller pool of available repair opportunities. Large MSOs such as Boyd can potentially offset those market pressures through acquisitions, expanded geographic coverage, insurer relationships and operational efficiencies.

For independent collision repair operators, however, the continued decline in claims volume reinforces the importance of monitoring car counts, controlling expenses and maintaining profitability when repair opportunities are limited.

Boyd ended the third quarter with 1,329 collision repair locations, an increase of 31% from 1,014 locations a year earlier. The company added 289 locations during the first nine months of 2026, including 258 through multi-location acquisitions, 17 through single-shop acquisitions and 14 startup facilities.
During the third quarter alone, Boyd acquired 10 single-shop locations.
The company’s continued expansion also underscores the role consolidation is playing in reshaping the collision repair marketplace, even as overall industry demand remains under pressure.
Profitability Improves Through Cost Savings
Boyd also reported improved profitability during the quarter, driven largely by its Project 360 operational improvement initiative and synergies associated with the Joe Hudson’s acquisition.
Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) increased 34.3% to $132.1 million, compared to $98.4 million during the third quarter of 2025.
Adjusted EBITDA margins improved to 13% from 12.4% a year earlier, while gross margins increased to 46.7% from 46.3%.

Boyd attributed its improved gross margins to higher paint margins, acquisition synergies and improved profitability in sublet operations, vehicle scanning and ADAS calibration. Those improvements were partially offset by lower labor and parts margins.

The gains in scanning and calibration margins are particularly noteworthy as collision repair businesses increasingly look to diagnostics, ADAS-related operations and other services to improve profitability.

Through the first nine months of 2026, Boyd realized $50 million in cost savings from Project 360 and acquisition synergies. The company expects another $15 million in savings during the fourth quarter, bringing its projected full-year total to $65 million.

Despite its higher revenue and adjusted operating earnings, Boyd reported net earnings of just $81,000 for the quarter, compared to $10.8 million a year earlier. The company attributed the decline to acquisition and transformation costs, along with higher amortization of intangible assets.
Boyd’s outlook suggests collision repairers should remain cautious about expecting a near-term rebound in repairable insurance claims.

Although the company reported continued positive same-store sales growth in October, it emphasized that monthly and quarterly fluctuations should not be viewed as reliable indicators of longer-term market trends.
Boyd also expects to open 11 additional startup locations during the fourth quarter, continuing its expansion strategy despite the challenging claims environment.

For the broader collision repair industry, the company’s results reinforce two competing trends: Repairable claims volumes remain below prior-year levels, while large MSOs continue to expand their footprints and capture additional market share.

The distinction is particularly important for independent collision repair facilities. Boyd’s 2.2% same-store sales growth, achieved against an estimated 1% to 3% decline in industry repairable claims, suggests the company is outperforming the market rather than benefiting from a widespread recovery in repair demand.
And with Boyd incorporating continued claims declines into its long-term planning assumptions, the latest results offer little indication that the industry’s car-count challenges are nearing an end.
For more information on Boyd Group, visit boydgroup.com.

articles.title: On Target continues taking a look at SRS repair procedures
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: Bronco SRS information from Volumes 2 and 3 is found in “Section 501-20B: Supplemental Restraint System, Description and Operation” of the Ford Workshop Manual (WSM).
On Target warns that incorrect repair techniques or actions can cause SRS to deploy accidentally.
“Never compromise or depart from these instructions,” On Target states. “Failure to precisely follow all instructions could result in serious personal injury from an accidental deployment.”

Before installing a safety canopy or side air curtain assembly, repairers should inspect the roofline for any damage because sheet metal may need to be reworked to its original condition and structural integrity. Repairers need to inspect fasteners for damage. If damaged, replace them and remove any foreign material.

“Failure to follow these instructions may result in the safety canopy or side air curtain deploying incorrectly, which increases the risk of serious personal injury or death in a crash,” On Target states.
How SRS is repowered depends on whether a fault was present at the beginning of the repair. If it is, reinstall the body control module (BCM) power fuse(s).

To determine whether a fault is present, verify that all airbags are installed and connected and the ignition is off. Then, wait 10 seconds and start the car. The airbag warning indicator should continuously illuminate for 6 seconds, then turn off. It’ll take about another 3o seconds from that point for the restraints control module (RCM) to complete SRS testing.
After 30 seconds, if the indicator fails to light, remains lit continuously, or flashes, an SRS fault exists.
More detail on both scenarios is available in Volume 3. Ford said additional SRS diagrams and repair details will be provided in future
volumes of On Target, focusing on pyrotechnic device disposal and more.
Previous installments on this repair are found in On Target’s 2025 volumes 3 and 4 and 2026 volume 1.
For more in-depth repair information on this and other Ford and Lincoln vehicles, refer to the WSM at FordServiceInfo.com, and check back often as repair procedures can be updated without notice.
Volume 3 also wraps up a series on rear-rail sectioning and includes the second article of a new “focus series” on seatbelt system inspections.

Specific steps are provided for Ford Explorer rear-rail sectioning as demonstrated in the I-CAR Repairers Realm video series. Previous installments are available in On Target 2025, Volume 4, and 2026 Volumes 1 and 2.

For the seatbelt series, On Target states that each article includes overviews of numerous WSM subsections on the topic, using the 2026 Expedition as an example vehicle. Volume 3 covers additional system operation and component descriptions from Section 501-20A.

articles.title: Jane Kim declares victory in California Insurance Commissioner race
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: Jane Kim has declared victory in the California Insurance Commissioner race after a tight race delayed final results.
As of Sunday, Kim had 53.1% of the votes. Her opponent, Ben Allen, had 46.9%, with some precincts still reporting.

“California, thank you,” Kim said on an Instagram post Friday. “ I am so honored to be your next Insurance Commissioner. We ran against millions of dollars, the entire political establishment, and the odds. And we won. For working families, and to make insurance affordable, available, and fair. I can’t wait to get started.”
Allen also posted on social media, saying he had called Kim to congratulate her.
“Jane ran a strong race and it appears that she has run,” Allen says. “I desperately want her to succeed, because if she succeeds, the state succeeds.
Political Action Committees (PACs) have contributed a record $6 million in campaign donations to the California Insurance Commission race, according to a CalMatters report.
The article says this includes $3.2 million to support Allen and $1.5 million to oppose Kim.

Kim previously served on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, as California political director for Bernie Sanders, and as California director for the Working Families Party, according to her campaign website.
Her priorities focus on “affordable, available insurance for all,” the website states. She proposes a single-payer disaster insurance policy for state residents.
The website also says she’ll ensure premiums cover claims, or lower them.

“Insurance companies should spend premium dollars on their intended purpose: protecting policyholders,” the website states. “If companies collect more than they need to cover claims and a reasonable profit, that money should go back to policyholders or be invested in statewide resilience, not huge payouts at our expense — like the $27 million salary one insurance company CEO was paid last year.”
Georgia, Oklahoma and Kansas also elected new insurance commissioners during the mid-term election.

articles.title: Federal Reserve senior policy advisor: Collision shops at front lines of auto industry changes
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: As the U.S. auto industry faces multiple disruptions, collision repairers are on the front lines of observing how consumers respond to changes in a sector critical to the nation’s gross domestic product (GDP), Kristen Dziczek, senior policy advisor at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said during The Industry Exchange at the Collision Industry Conference in Las Vegas.
“I think your shop is really where this broad economy meets people’s pocketbooks,” Dziczek said. “You’re seeing that decision made right on the front lines.”
Dziczek says those collision shop experiences will tell a story about the economy before data shows it.

“You’re seeing how trade increases the price of the part shipping,” Dziczek said. “You’re seeing how technology changes the things you have to do for calibration and the arguments you have to have about paying for those sorts of things. You’re seeing how finances change to higher deductibles; how the loss per mile is lower, but the loss per collision is higher.”
Part of Dziczek’s job is to have conversations with those throughout the auto industry, including collision repair businesses, about what they are seeing in the economy, she said.

“There’s a bunch of really smart people who are doing very complicated mathematical models of the economy, and we listen to all of that, and then they say, ‘And now, what’s really going on in the economy?’” she said.

Dziczek has been working at the Federal Reserve for about five years. Previously, she worked at General Motors, the UAW, in various auto industry roles for Congress, and at a nonprofit auto industry think tank.
“I think I have the coolest job in the auto industry,” she added.

Auto makes up about 5% of the U.S. GDP and employs more than 1 million people, Dziczek explained. She added that the industry touches all the “big moving parts,” like steel, aluminum, copper, microchips, oil, critical minerals, and magnets.

“We’ve got lenders, we’ve got insurers, we’ve got repair, we’ve got customers,” Dziczek said. “We’re [Federal Reserve] looking at consumer behavior, we’re looking at banking behavior, we’re looking at all sorts of things through the lens of the auto industry. It’s super duper important, and there are very few other segments of the economy that are 5% of the GDP.”

During the Industry Exchange, Aaron Schulenburg, executive director of the Society of Collision Repair Specialists (SCRS), asked Dziczek about the current and possible future pressures on the auto industry.
In 2026, gas prices, vehicle sales, tariffs, EVs, and technologies were some of the developments that the Federal Reserve paid attention to, she said.

“I’ll say this isn’t the highest gas prices have ever been, but it is the highest they’ve ever been this time of year,” Dziczek said as she ran through the list. “Sales have been remarkably resilient, coming in around $16 million this year. Consumers keep buying, so there’s been not really any kind of pullback with that. We’ve seen a few little blips from supply chain disruptions here and there, and then of course tariffs and how tariffs have played out.”

When discussing consumer spending, she said buyers seem to “be fine.” However, she added that new car buyers tend to make six-figure incomes. She added that there are some troubling signs with auto delinquencies, adding that they are at the highest level since 2010.
Dziczek said the EV reset has shifted focus to hybrids. Currently, about 16.7% of the vehicle market is hybrid, and some vehicles only have a hybrid configuration.
Electrified vehicles overall are about 24% of the market.
“That EV reset, however, burned about $100 billion in capital for the automakers,” Dziczek said. “A huge, huge turnaround, while the rest of the world continues on in electrification.”
Schulenburg asked if there are other vehicle technologies that the Federal Reserve is watching.
In response, Dziczek said two technologies that are most important to the collision repair industry: manufacturing changes to fewer parts and ADAS/automation.
Automakers are following Tesla’s lead on gigacasting to make vehicles less expensive, she said.
This year, Ford has been at the forefront of the conversation about gigacasting (or megacasting as Ford refers to it).

The automaker announced it would invest $5 billion to change how it makes electric vehicles to lower its EV prices. The target starting price for a mid-sized EV truck is $30,000 compared to the average EV cost of $56,000, according to CBS News.

The shift includes changing how the assembly line operates and a reduction in the total number of parts used in the vehicle. For example, a Ford press release says the wiring harness will be 4,000 feet shorter.
Dziczek said replacing many parts with fewer parts does make vehicles easier to manufacture but “maybe not easier to repair.”
It also could have implications for the companies that make the parts being reduced by the automakers.
ADAS and automation are changing the industry in other ways, she said. This includes federal regulatory actions and conversation.
In September, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) announced an agreement with SAE to expedite the development of data-driven AV performance standards.
In March, NHTSA also announced plans to research ways to update its autonomous driving regulations.
The agency also mandated automatic emergency brakes as standard in vehicles by 2029.
ADAS features do come with a cost, Dziczek said.
“Sure, my car can’t crash, but when the car that can crash runs into it, that bumper is very expensive,” she said.
For collision repairers, this means calibrations, she said.
Dziczek also said technology is changing how vehicles are manufactured.
Automakers are using AI from beginning to end, she said. This includes product design, supply chains, engineering, manufacturing quality, safety, and in the product itself, she added.

She shared an example of an automaker building a check engine light that tells consumers the vehicle is trending out of spec. It then sets up an appointment and can order parts with a push of the button on the dashboard.
There are parts of the manufacturing process that are already lights out, Dziczek said.
A recent federal study found that manufacturing is slightly lower in AI use than other business sectors but that it is rapidly increasing its use, she said.
“The rate of change is about double that of the overall economy,” Dziczek adds.
Schulenburg asked whether technology could change productivity and cost of producing vehicles.

“I think some of that’s up to consumers,” She replied. “If you get greater productivity, which technology should bring you, you have scale, which means you’re not just making a few cars that way. You are changing really quickly and can lower costs, but savings come about through market forces, policy, and consumer decisions.”
Consumers are choosing vehicles with more features.
“You’re still spending more dollars because you’re loading it up with features,” she added.
Other costs can also show up after purchasing a vehicle, including insurance, maintenance, and repair.
Labor costs and labor availability are part of driving repair costs, she added. The rates can change for different brands, repair types, and the cost of the parts.
Insurance is also a complicated set of constructs, she said. Consumers sometimes don’t realize the consequences of lowering their insurance costs.
Schulenburg asked how the Federal Reserve distinguishes an underlying product that becomes more complex and expensive from the broader inflationary pressure.

Dziczek replied that the Federal Reserve looks at things that are inflationary or products that are risking costs over time. One-time shocks, such as increased prices post-COVID, are seen as transitory, she added.
“We’re looking at things that build a sustained growth,” Dziczek said.
Fuel costs aren’t necessarily inflationary right now, but that could change because of all the places it comes through the economy, she said.
The closing of the Strait of Hormuz is an event that could cause a one-time shock or create an inflationary event that ripples through multiple industries, she added.
Aluminum, which currently has a 50% tariff, passes through the strait, she said. She added that helium also comes from the region, which is used to make microchips.

“We take fuel, obviously, which goes into our gas tanks, but also goes into the plastics that we use in the vehicle, and then it goes into the diesel trucks that bring the parts to the factory and the ships and runs factories in other countries that don’t have big energy emergency supplies,” Dziczek said. “Taiwan, for example, there’s only limited supply or places to store energy on the island of Taiwan. So if you get an energy shock to Taiwan and you can’t make chips, big problem.”
However, right now, auto price increases have remained modest, up 1.5% last month. This is down from overall inflation at about 3.7%, she said.
Tariffs so far have only created a one-time shock rather than an inflationary event, Dziczek said.

“The tariffs didn’t keep going up month after month,” she said. “They went up once, and actually they kind of got negotiated down over time, or there were exceptions to the rules that came into place, so there was a spike, and then it came back down.”

There is a threat that tariffs will be increased to 50% on autos and parts from Canada Jan. 1, she added. That also wouldn’t be inflationary unless it became 75% the next month and 100% the following month.

Election results were not in while Dziczek spoke on Tuesday; however, she said any changes from the election could affect tariffs and regulations. The changes could also affect budgetary policies, she added.
Schulenburg asked if the competitive position of the automotive industry in the U.S. changed as other countries have expanded their capabilities.
“China is the number one exporter of vehicles, 7.1 million vehicles last year,” Dziczek said. “But the U.S. is effectively walled off from China and Chinese brands.”
Global automakers are competing abroad, she said.

For example, Chinese-built vehicles were about 4% of the Mexican market, she added. She explained that not all are Chinese brands. Some Western brands that lost share in China have been exported to other markets.
“They’ve really become a big force in global vehicle production, and even without that direct competition in the U.S. market,” Dziczek said.

She noted that intense competition in China has caused manufacturers to develop vehicles really fast. It’s often believed that the vehicles are lower cost because of subsidies and governments behind them. Yet, she added that a recent study found that when BYD was compared to Tesla, there was only a 5% cost differential from subsidies.
The rest of the cost savings comes from controlling the supply chain from batteries to minerals to cells, she said.
“They have immense scale and dominance in batteries,” Dziczek said. “They don’t just make EVs, though; I’ll point out they also have immense vertical integration.”
She added that China also has density in its supply chain. A lot of what is needed to build a vehicle is in China.
Because of the high competition, Chinese manufacturers are also developing vehicles faster than in the U.S.
“Their development from paper to vehicle on the road is less than two to three years,” she said.
It can take five to seven years in the U.S., she said.

“One thing that’s interesting about two to three years is that your policy environment is probably more stable over the next two to three years,” she added. “Like we know who the president is for the next two years.”
The U.S. automakers can’t make a vehicle 100% in the U.S., she said. For example, Nvidia chips can’t be made in the country.
The country is seeing some shifts in assembly, she said. Multiple automakers, including GM, Stellantis, and Audi, have announced production investments in the U.S.

“Since the tariffs went into effect, we’ve seen an uptick of about 6,500 manufacturing jobs in the motor vehicle assembly sector,” Dziczek said. “The parts sector has lost jobs for 32 straight months, down about 10,400.”
As parts companies come back, they are turning to automation and AI, she added.
Schulenburg asked which economic indicators Dziczek will be watching in 2027.

“The renegotiation of USMCA and whether we’d get to some kind of a trade truce with Canada and Mexico that settles things down and gives some more stability to the investment environment,” Dziczek answered.
The pace of sales, transaction prices, and employment is always at the top of the list, she added.
Dziczek said another thing to watch is auto credit delinquencies, lending standards, and what is happening to rates.
Repair costs versus insurance gaps is also on the list, she said.

“Income growth has dropped below the inflation rate, so when wages are growing faster than inflation, that’s good,” Dziczek said. “When wages are growing more slowly than inflation, that might cause people to become more conservative.”
If people stop making big purchases, auto plant workers wouldn’t make cars, she explained.
“It starts this spiral downward,” she said.
The collision repair industry should be looking at its labor pipeline, Dziczek said.
“How you’re going to get people to do this work because this is not offshore work,” she said. “This is work that technology can change, but it’s not going offshore.”
Aaron Schulenburg, SCRS executive director and Kristen Dziczek, senior policy advisor at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, discuss the automotive industry during CIC in Las Vegas Nov. 3, 2026.

articles.title: Celebrating the Women Who Move Our Industry Forward
articles.author: Brandi Gangel

paras.en: There are plenty of reasons to love AAPEX. The innovation, the energy, the business opportunities, and of course, the people. Wednesday morning’s breakfast, the kickoff to Wednesday, Women in Auto Care offered a particularly meaningful reminder of what makes the automotive aftermarket such a special industry to be part of.

The Women in Auto Care Annual Networking Breakfast and Awards program brought together an incredible community of industry professionals to celebrate the women making a difference in our businesses, our industry, and in the lives of those around them.

Throughout the morning, as award recipients took the stage, a common theme emerged. Despite their different career paths, experiences, and accomplishments, nearly every woman spoke about the same thing: the people who helped them get where they are today.

The mentors who saw potential before they saw it in themselves. The colleagues who became lifelong friends. The families who supported big dreams, long hours, and bold decisions. And the women who opened doors, offered encouragement, and made room for others at the table. It was a powerful reminder that while individual accomplishments deserve to be celebrated, very few of us get where we are entirely on our own.

One particularly touching moment came from a young award recipient who spoke about her three-year-old daughter growing up surrounded by strong women in automotive. To her daughter, the industry isn’t male dominated, it’s simply a place where her mom, her grandmother, and countless other women belong, contribute, and succeed. What an incredible perspective. And what a wonderful reflection of the progress this organization continues to make.

Another recipient shared the story of her grandmother, who helped operate a family service station decades ago but was overlooked when the business received industry recognition. Generations later, today, her granddaughter stood on stage accepting a Shop Owner of the Year Award, dedicating the honor to the woman who helped inspire her.

And in a memorable moment of audience participation, another honoree distributed tiny pink army women, encouraging attendees to keep one as a reminder of their own strength and give another to someone who could use a little encouragement. A simple gesture with a powerful message: We all have an army behind us, and we have an opportunity to be part of someone else’s.

These stories were different, but their message was remarkably consistent. Success isn’t only measured by titles, accomplishments, or recognition, it’s also measured by the opportunities we create, the relationships we build, and the people we help along the way. That’s what makes Women in Auto Care so special.

It has built a community where women genuinely celebrate one another’s successes, encourage each other’s ambitions, and invest in the next generation of leaders. A big congratulations to all this year’s award winners and finalists. And to the Women in Auto Care organization, its leadership, volunteers, allies and supporters, thank you for creating opportunities to recognize women and champion their contributions to our industry.

articles.title: Momentum USA Launches 77 Brake Part Numbers
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Momentum USA announced that it has introduced 77 new part numbers in August. European, Asian and electric vehicles are among those covered by the new part numbers.
- 36 new part numbers in the AmeriStar brake pad line, which cover 28.7 million vehicles in operation. Impact applications include high-volume Hyundai/Kia platforms.

- 8 new part numbers covering 8.8 million VIO in the AmeriPlatinum Ceramic line. This line now provides late-model coverage for import cars like the Toyota Corolla/Prius, Hyundai Palisade and Kia Telluride.
- 14 new E-Marked R90 Euro Coated Rotor and fully coated rotor additions in the AmeriPro line. This release covers BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Land Rover, Volvo, Genesis and Mini models.
- Seven new EPS Friction brake pad SKUs, extending high-performance stopping power to applications like Alfa Romeo, BMW 2/3/4 Series, Maserati, Porsche Cayenne and Jaguar F-Pace.
- New numbers across AmeriPRO and VGX add coverage for electric and late-model crossover models like the Nissan Leaf.

articles.title: Worldpac to Open Automated Distribution Center
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Worldpac announced plans to open its first automated distribution center, a new 413,000-square-foot facility in Forest Park, Georgia. Scheduled to begin operations in the first half of 2027, the facility will feature AutoStore robotic storage and retrieval technology.

The facility will support Worldpac branches and customers across the Southeast and surrounding markets, while providing more than 250,000 additional square feet compared with the current Norcross distribution center, the company said.

AutoStore is an automated storage and retrieval system that uses robotics to store, retrieve, and process inventory within a highly efficient storage grid. Rather than team members traveling through warehouse aisles to locate parts, inventory is automatically delivered to workstations for picking, replenishment, and processing.
The facility will be located at 2160 Anvil Block Road, Suite 200 Forest Park, GA 30297.

“We are excited to expand Worldpac’s distribution presence in the Atlanta metro market and strengthen our ability to serve customers throughout the Southeastern United States. The Forest Park facility represents a major step forward in our use of robotics and automation, helping us improve speed, accuracy, and efficiency,” said Rich Tannenbaum, chief operating officer of Worldpac.

articles.title: Advics Offers More Aftermarket Brake Pads, Rotors
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Advics announced the availability of 56 new brake pad kit SKUs and three new disc brake rotor SKUs.

The 56 new ultra-premium brake pad kit SKUs provide approximately 62.8 million vehicles in operation (VIO) axle coverage in the U.S. and Canada. The expansion covers Acura, Honda, Infiniti, Mazda, Mitsubishi, Nissan, Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, Chrysler, Dodge, Ford, GMC, Jeep, Lincoln, Ram, Genesis, Hyundai and Kia applications.
Advics is also expanding its ultra-premium disc brake rotor line with three new SKUs for Toyota and Lexus applications, providing approximately 858,000 VIO axle coverage in the U.S. and Canada.
All three rotor SKUs are manufactured in the U.S.

articles.title: Niterra President and CEO Mike Schwab on ‘Delivering Trusted Solutions’
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: This episode of DriveTime features Mike Schwab, president and CEO of Niterra North America, Inc.

Schwab said Niterra has evolved well beyond its roots as an ignition specialist while maintaining the quality and reliability associated with its NGK brand. Today, Niterra’s automotive portfolio extends beyond spark plugs to include ignition coils, wire sets, NTK oxygen and technical sensors and rotating electrical products such as starters and alternators.

Schwab emphasized that quality, integrity, teamwork and consistent execution remain fundamental to Niterra’s business strategy, even as the industry evolves. These principles, he says, guide how the company serves customers, from delivering dependable products and maintaining transparency to strengthening partnerships and addressing customer challenges. Schwab emphasized that execution means consistently delivering on commitments involving product availability, customer service and new product introductions. While technology and product offerings will continue to change, he believes trust, reliability and strong customer relationships will remain essential to the company’s long-term success.

paras.en: Looking ahead, Schwab said the transition from NGK Spark Plug to Niterra represents a broader transformation rather than simply a name change. Opportunities in advanced mobility, electric vehicles and other emerging technologies are part of that strategy. Schwab said the Niterra name, derived from Latin words meaning “to shine” and “Earth,” reflects the company’s ambition to contribute to a more sustainable future.

articles.title: The Wheel Group Names Nick Garza Territory Sales Manager
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: The Wheel Group (TWG), designer, developer and owner of aftermarket wheel, tire, accessory and off-road brands, named Nick Garza as territory sales manager, based at TWG’s Columbus, Ohio, branch. Garza brings 18 years of automotive industry experience and a track record in leadership, customer service and business development.

Garza joins TWG following an 18-year career with Discount Tire, where he advanced through a series of leadership positions, ultimately serving as an operations manager, according to TWG. Throughout his career, he developed experience in retail operations, customer service, team development and business performance, building an understanding of what it takes to run a successful automotive business.
Role Focused on Dealer Relationships and Growth

In his new role at TWG, Garza will work directly with dealers and customers throughout his territory to strengthen relationships, develop new business and connect customers with TWG’s portfolio of aftermarket wheels, tires, accessories and off-road products. His background in retail operations and team leadership will help dealers identify opportunities, grow their businesses and better serve their customers, TWG said.

“We’re excited to welcome Nick to TWG,” said Chance Martin, director of sales, Northeast. “He brings a tremendous amount of experience, and he understands the business from the ground up. His background in operations, customer service and developing people will be a real asset as we continue building our team and growing our business across the Northeast.”
Garza is equally enthusiastic about joining TWG and the opportunities ahead.

“After 18 years in the industry, I’m excited to take on a new challenge and bring my experience to The Wheel Group,” said Garza. “I have always believed that success comes down to taking care of customers, developing strong teams, and building relationships that last. TWG has an impressive portfolio of brands and lots of room to grow, and I am looking forward to working with our dealers, learning their businesses, and helping them take advantage of the opportunities ahead.”
Continued Investment in Sales Organization

Garza’s addition reflects TWG’s continued investment in its sales organization and its commitment to providing customers with knowledgeable, accessible sales support. As the company introduces new products, expands its brand portfolio and develops resources that help dealers compete and grow, it said its territory sales team remains a critical link between TWG and its customers.

articles.title: Fleet Costs, Uptime Lead ACT Expo 2027 Agenda
articles.author: Kevin Linger

paras.en: Organizers opened registration for ACT Expo 2027 and released a conference agenda focused on fuel costs, maintenance, safety, and equipment purchasing. The conference will run May 17-20, 2027, at the Las Vegas Convention Center. Early bird rates are available through Dec. 11, 2026.
Fuel Efficiency, Maintenance and Equipment Decisions

The ACT Expo 2027 agenda will cover how fleets can reduce fuel use through diesel engine technology, aerodynamics, and matching vehicles to their workloads. Sessions will also examine how fleets use connected vehicle data and predictive tools to plan maintenance and improve uptime.

Other discussions will address how changing emissions requirements could affect vehicle purchases, maintenance, and replacement cycles. The program will include fleet case studies and technical workshops on topics such as driver-assistance systems, commercial deployments of autonomous vehicles, alternative fuel availability, and charging infrastructure.
The conference will offer continuing education credit opportunities for a second year. Organizers will announce which sessions and workshops are eligible as those details are finalized.
Exhibit Hall, Ride & Drive and Registration

The exhibit hall will be open May 18-19. Organizers expect more than 400 exhibitors and sponsors and more than 200 commercial vehicles on display, including light-, medium-, and heavy-duty trucks, vans, buses, and off-road equipment.
At the Ride & Drive, attendees will be able to assess vehicle handling and driver comfort and ask manufacturer representatives about maintenance, range, and infrastructure requirements.

Fleets and shippers that buy two passes can receive additional passes for qualifying team members. The organization said eligible first-time fleet and shipper attendees may also qualify for a complimentary pass. Terms are available on the registration page.

articles.title: Art Fisher Award for Excellence in Education Given to Corey Bartlett
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: The Aftermarket Warehouse Distributors Association (AWDA), a community of the Auto Care Association, presented the 2026 Art Fisher Award for Excellence in Education, to Corey Bartlett, CEO of Auto Parts Headquarters (APH) based in St. Cloud, Minnesota. The award was presented on November 1st by AWDA Vice Chair Young Suhr at AWDA’s 2026 Annual Conference in Las Vegas.

AWDA’s Art Fisher Award for Excellence in Education is presented annually to an aftermarket company or individual that demonstrates outstanding commitment to education and training, either within their organization or throughout the industry. Given in memory of former AWDA Chairman Art Fisher, the award grants scholarships in the name of the award winner to two students enrolled in the automotive aftermarket management program at Northwood University. AWDA Vice Chair Young Suhr presented the award.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Bartlett has prioritized education throughout his career at APH. Within his first 10 years, he reorganized staff and expanded employee training. He completed the University of the Aftermarket’s Leadership 2010 program and earned Automotive Aftermarket Professional and Master Automotive Aftermarket Professional designations in 2002 and 2009.

“Corey has shown incredible initiative in supporting training and continuing education,” said John R. Washbish, president and CEO, Aftermarket Auto Parts Alliance, Inc. “Through his leadership roles and example, he has consistently improved the education and standards of his staff, the Alliance, and the industry as a whole.”

As CEO, Bartlett and his managers developed a 101-level course to help employees understand APH’s expansion into medium-duty, heavy-duty and agricultural segments. A partnership with a local technical college added hands-on experience, with nearly 100% participation among the company’s 1,200 employees. Corey also helped oversee the Alliance scholarship program and create its Technician of the Year program.

His industry service includes chairing the AWDA Board of Governors, mentoring through the Young Auto Care Networking Group and supporting the Auto Care Political Action Committee. He was the 2017 AWDA Pursuit of Excellence honoree and supports WACOSA and other local nonprofits.

articles.title: Advance Auto Parts Opens First Store in Richboro, Pa.
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: and expertise for local drivers and automotive professionals. The company marked the opening of the store at 1039 2nd Street Pike with a ribbon-cutting ceremony alongside local officials and representatives from Middle Bucks Institute of Technology who were on site to accept a donation for the school’s automotive technology program.

The donation will help students gain hands-on experience, training, and career opportunities through the school’s automotive technology programs. Skilled automotive technicians continue to be in high demand, with approximately 70,000 openings projected annually through 2034, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

“Opening our first store in Richboro is an exciting milestone for our team,” said Eli Rosa, regional vice president, Advance Auto Parts. “We’re grateful for the opportunity to serve this community and proud to support students at Middle Bucks Institute of Technology as they pursue hands-on learning and explore careers in the automotive field.”

“We appreciate Advance Auto Parts‘ support of our automotive technology program,” said Dr. Mark Covelle, administrative director at Middle Bucks Institute of Technology. “Donations like this help support hands-on learning opportunities for our students as they build skills and prepare for future careers in the industry.”

articles.title: GSP Launches All-New, Core-Free Brake Caliper Line
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: GSP North America announced the GSP ADVANTEDGE Brake Caliper program, an all-new caliper range that frees distributors from the cost and hassle of managing cores. It’s on display at AAPEX, booth #F14611.
Every caliper is entirely new, distributors no longer need to handle, store, sort and ship cores back to the supplier, GSP said.
Every unit is built from the ground up with OE-matched components:
- Precision-cast ductile iron or aluminum bodies and carrier brackets, with precision-machined surfaces and threads
- OE-specified phenolic or steel pistons to match each braking system
- OE-grade EPDM seals and boots that hold piston pressure and keep contaminants out
- Installation hardware included: copper washers, new banjo bolt and abutment clips
- 100% end-of-line pressure and leak validated before leaving the factory
The initial range covers more than 80% of category demand and is expected to reach 95% within 12 months of its formal launch at AAPEX.

The range is produced at GSP’s new manufacturing facility in Malaysia. GSP’s distribution partners can expect the same high-level quality and execution they have experienced in all GSP lines, the company said.

“The GSP ADVANTEDGE Brake Caliper program is designed to improve distributors’ operational performance, increase bay throughput through enhanced quality and, ultimately, give customers restored and reliable braking performance,” said Tom Galla, director of new products for GSP North America.

articles.title: 'The possibilities are truly breathtaking': NASA's Roman Space Telescope will take better images and last longer than experts predicted
articles.author: Harry Baker

paras.en: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine — which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex — successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.
The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."
The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.
The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.
All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

articles.title: The Grand Canyon is missing over a billion years of rocks. Now scientists know why.
articles.author: Stephanie Pappas

paras.en: More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion, which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: "We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics, said Shanan Peters, a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction — when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters, said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.
Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.
"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.
"So far in Africa and Russia, we don’t have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."
Editor's Note: This story was updated at 10:30 p.m. E.D.T. to note that James Price, not Tia Ghose, edited this story.

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

articles.title: 2,200-year-old gold bear figurine and surprising number of bones found in massive burial mound in Kazakhstan
articles.author: Margherita Bassi

paras.en: Archaeologists in Kazakhstan have discovered a unique gold bear figurine in a 2,200-year-old burial mound that looters had hit but failed to empty completely.

The sculpted bear stands on its hind limbs and holds a pot-like container between its front paws. The artifact would have been worn as part of a headdress, and holes at its base indicate that it could have been sewn onto the garment, according to a translated statement from the Kazakhstan government.

The gold bear was unearthed at an Early Iron Age burial mound at the Karagaily burial ground in the southern city of Almaty, along with a surprisingly high number of human bones for a single burial mound.
Although other gold-crafted animals have been found in the region, the newly unearthed bear is the first of its kind.

"The sculpted bear figurine is unique to Kazakhstan. No similar finds have been discovered previously," Lyazzat Sagyndykova, director of the Almaty Museums Association, which conducted the excavation, said in the statement. "This discovery allows us to trace cultural parallels across the whole of Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to Altai."

The figurine dates to the Saka period, named for a nomadic horseback-riding people from Iran who lived on the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin of what is now western China. Archaeologists have found comparable gold objects at other excavations in Kazakhstan, according to the statement. For example, a headdress element shaped like a small leopard previously came to light at the Almaty Kok-Kainar burial ground, which dates to the fourth century B.C. Also, the headdress of Kazakhstan's famous "Golden Man," a young Iron Age warrior buried in an extraordinarily lavish grave, also has a gold, sheep-shaped decorative element.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It's unclear which bear species the figurine depicts, but today Kazakhstan is home to two subspecies of brown bear: the Tien Shan or Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus), which lives in the Tien Shan Mountains in the southeast, and the East Siberian brown bear (Ursus arctos collaris) in the Altai Mountains in the east, according to a study published earlier this year.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Preliminary analyses date the recently excavated site to the fourth to third centuries B.C., according to the statement. Based on the number of bones they excavated, experts suspect that the mound, which is around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and roughly 85 feet (26 m) wide, may have been the final resting place for four adults and three children.

"Of particular interest is the unusually large number of human remains in a single burial mound, as such burials are atypical for Kazakhstan," Marat Mugalovich Nurpeisov, a senior research fellow at the Almaty Museums Association, said in the statement. "As a rule, burial mounds of a comparable size were intended for the burial of one or two people."

Archaeologists also found pieces of Saka pottery, most of which had been strewn about after the burial had been looted in ancient times, according to the statement. The thieves left behind a 10-foot (3 m) looting pit.

"Research into the Karagaily burial ground is ongoing," Nurpeisov said in the statement. "To clarify the circumstances of the burial and determine the exact number of individuals interred, further analyses are planned, including the involvement of anthropologists."
After all of the investigations are finished, some of the artifacts will be put on display at the Almaty Museum, according to the statement.

Margherita is a trilingual freelance writer specializing in science and history writing with a particular interest in archaeology, palaeontology, astronomy and human behavior. She earned her BA from Boston College in English literature, ancient history and French, and her journalism MA from L'École Du Journalisme de Nice in International New Media Journalism. In addition to Live Science, her bylines include Smithsonian Magazine, Discovery Magazine, BBC Travel, Atlas Obscura and more.
