articles.title: Even Replacing Some of Your Dietary Dairy With Plant-Based Alternatives Can Lead to Nutrient Deficiencies, Study Suggests

paras.en: Alternative dairy products are widely available in many countries. Grocery stores and cafes frequently offer “milks” made from soy, almond, oat, rice or other crops. That’s good news for people who don’t consume dairy, as well as for our planet, since the production of plant-based milk is more environmentally friendly than regular milk.

But relying on these plant-based alternatives—even partially—might carry health risks. In a study published in the September issue of the journal Lancet Planetary Health, researchers ran computer simulations based on United Kingdom nutrition data and found that swapping standard dairy for vegan versions can lead to deficiencies of four vital nutrients. However, that could be combated by mandating that nutrients be added to plant-based dairy alternatives, as well as bread, making them fortified foods.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Vegan milks, cheeses, yogurts, ice creams and more are becoming increasingly popular as people turn to them for health or sustainability reasons. However, they often lack certain nutrients found in dairy.

To explore the potential public health implications, researchers pulled data from the U.K.’s National Diet and Nutrition Survey involving more than 3,500 people between the ages of 1.5 and 100 years old. They put that information into a computer model to simulate how swapping out regular milk, yogurt and cheese with commercially available plant-based versions affected intake of four micronutrients: iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12.

The results weren’t great. Even replacing a modest amount of dairy caused a decline in intake of all analyzed micronutrients. Iodine took the biggest hit. Your thyroid gland needs iodine to make certain hormones, and it’s also crucial for brain development. The micronutrient is especially important for infants, adolescents and pregnant people.

The survey data revealed that 54 percent of girls ages 14 to 18 weren’t eating enough iodine. Replacing just 35 percent of dairy with plant-based alternatives would cause the deficiency to jump to 65 percent. Similarly, 32 percent of women ages 19 to 49 were iodine deficient at baseline, and it would rise to 42 percent after the same dairy swap.
If dairy intake was completely replaced, 80 percent of teenage girls and 72 percent of teenage boys would be iodine deficient, according to the computer simulations.
Did you know? Other drivers of iodine deficiency

In recent years, many people have been replacing their typical table salt with trendier versions, like Himalayan, sea and kosher. However, that’s contributing to a rise in iodine deficiency, since table salt is often fortified with the micronutrient.

“A strength of the study is that it looks at partial replacement rather than only a complete switch, which better reflects how most people actually change their diets. It also breaks the results down by age and sex, which shows clearly who is most at risk,” says Ian Givens, director of the University of Reading’s Institute for Food, Nutrition and Health in England and a registered nutritionist, in an expert reaction compiled by the Science Media Centre.

However, “there are limitations,” adds Givens, who wasn’t involved in the study. “The findings are based on modeled reduction of dairy intake, so they show a risk of inadequacy rather than confirming deficiency but are still valuable data.”

Next, the researchers investigated whether fortification of vegan dairy products, as well as the staple food bread, might help avoid these predicted micronutrient deficiencies. The strategy worked. Computer simulations suggested that adding iodine to both types of food caused iodine deficiency to drop to 37 percent among teenage girls at 20 percent dairy replacement. And at a complete dairy swap, deficiency was projected to be at 43 percent among adolescent girls.
Ultimately, the team’s findings indicate that more foods should have fortification requirements.

“Nutrition policy must evolve in tandem with environmental targets,” study co-author Katie Nicol, a human nutrition researcher at the University of Surrey in England, says in a statement. “However, it is important that shifts towards more sustainable diets do not compromise on public health. Fortification of foods is one way that this could be achieved; however, government policy is needed to make this happen.”
The good news is that some companies are already doing this.

“For anyone choosing plant-based milk, I’d recommend checking the label and choosing one fortified with iodine, such as Alpro,” Nichola Ludlam-Raine, a registered dietitian and spokesperson for the British Dietetic Association, who did not participate in the study, tells the Guardian’s Ian Sample. She notes that organic drinks don’t contain added nutrients.

And all of Oatly’s unflavored, non-organic oat drinks contain added nutrients, including iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12, says Caroline Orfila Jenkins, the company’s vice president for science and technology, to the outlet. “This research underlines the importance of appropriate fortification as diets become more plant-based.”

articles.title: Humans May Have Been Getting High on Weed 2,800 Years Ago. Cannabis Seeds and Hair With Traces of THC Were Found in an Ancient Tomb

paras.en: Cannabis is one of the world’s most widely used psychoactive plants, with millions of people inhaling and ingesting it for its mind-altering effects. But new research suggests our current relationship with weed is nothing new.

A study published November 5 in the journal Science suggests humans have been getting high on weed for at least 2,800 years—centuries longer than previously thought. The findings seem to offer the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use.

Researchers have long been interested in how ancient people used cannabis. Yet studying it has proven tricky because plants are rarely preserved over long periods of time. Since cannabis has many uses, including the production of oil and fiber, it’s even more challenging to determine whether and when individuals were using it specifically to get high.

In 2017, archaeologists digging in southern Siberia discovered a huge 2,800-year-old tomb that contained the remains of several high-status individuals. The site, called Tunnug 1, is associated with the Scythians, a nomadic, horse-riding culture that occupied the Eurasian steppe from the ninth to the third century B.C.E.

Excavations turned up numerous artifacts, from weapons and animal statues to pieces of gold jewelry and horse gear. But the researchers also found nearly 1,500 whole or partial cannabis seeds at the site, as well as preserved human hair, which allowed them to explore whether the Scythians might have been getting high.

“It’s only so often as an archaeologist that you get to drug test a person that’s been dead for nearly 3,000 years,” lead author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern in Switzerland and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany, tells the New York Times’ Annie Roth.

Radiocarbon dating traced the seeds to the early eighth century B.C.E., around the same time the burial site is believed to have been constructed. The hair, meanwhile, tested positive for pot. Specifically, the strands contained cannabinol (CBN), a byproduct of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive compound in the plant. It also contained weaker chemical signatures consistent with THC.

Caspari tells the Associated Press’ Jamey Keaten and Philipp Jenne that it’s “extremely rare” for archaeologists to find “both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context.”

Together, the results suggest the Scythians were using cannabis for its intoxicating properties. The researchers also believe they intentionally deposited the seeds in the tomb, likely because they viewed cannabis as important.
“Things of value in the world of the living often made it into the burial context as an offering in this region,” Caspari tells Reuters’ Will Dunham.

The idea is further supported by a historic description of Scythian funeral practices. Per the Times, the Greek historian Herodotus wrote in 440 B.C.E. that the Scythians “take some of this hemp seed and, creeping under the felt coverings, throw it upon the red-hot stones; immediately it smokes and gives out such a vapor as no Greek vapor bath can exceed; the Scyths, delighted, shout for joy.”

Caspari tells Reuters that researchers were always “quite hesitant” to believe Herodotus’ writings, because he tended to “drift into the fantastic.” However, based on their recent findings, they now know that “at least some of his descriptions about the steppe peoples had some truth,” he adds.
Did you know? Earliest evidence of habitual drug use

In September, researchers reported the earliest evidence for habitual drug use ever discovered. In a cave in Indonesia, they found the teeth of an individual who appears to have habitually sucked on betel nuts roughly 16,000 to 25,000 years ago, possibly to soothe a toothache.

Until now, the earliest evidence of cannabis use came from a 2,500-year-old burial site in western China, where archaeologists discovered the remains of charred cannabis with high levels of THC. However, ancient people there may not have been using cannabis to get high—it’s possible they were burning it for some other reason, such as to mask the smell of death.

The new paper, with its analysis of both cannabis seeds and pot-laced human hair, provides a “smoking gun of evidence” that humans were using the plant for its intoxicating properties, Caspar Meyer, an archaeologist at Bard College who was not involved with the paper, tells Scientific American’s Mary Randolph.

Others are skeptical, though. Volker Auwärter, a forensic toxicologist at the Medical Center-University of Freiburg in Germany, tells the AP that the hair analysis is “scientifically weak” and that the strands could’ve picked up traces of cannabis from the surrounding plant material.

Nevertheless, the research team is continuing to investigate the Scythians’ cannabis use and cultivation practices, such as whether they were choosing to grow plants that had high levels of mind-altering THC. “We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples,” Caspari says in a statement. “DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon.”

It’s also unclear whether the Scythians used cannabis exclusively during funerals, or whether getting high was more of a regular, everyday practice. One possibility, the researchers speculate, is that cannabis use helped ease some of the tension surrounding burials, which may have involved human sacrifice. The surface of the tomb at Tunnug 1, for instance, is littered with horse and human bones.

“Since we have dozens of sacrificed horses and some potential human sacrifices, it might also have been used to sedate the victims before something bad happened to them—but we cannot prove that,” Caspari tells CNN’s Jack Guy.

articles.title: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch Has Accumulated So Many Microplastics They Might Be Changing the Color of the Ocean

paras.en: Out in the Pacific Ocean, halfway between California and Hawaii, lies a massive collection of human-made debris that spans an area roughly twice the size of Texas. Known as the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, its accumulation of microplastics has now grown so large that it seems to be changing the color of the ocean.

Twenty years of satellite data suggests that the water in and around the trash pile has become more blue-green. Though the researchers couldn’t confirm microplastics are behind the color shift, computer simulations hint that that is likely the case. The findings, published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment on November 5, could help experts identify the most heavily polluted areas of the ocean to guide cleanup efforts.

“It’s shocking and worrying,” says Aron Stubbins, a chemist and co-director of Northeastern University’s Plastics Center who wasn’t involved in the work, to Evan Bush at NBC News. “The fact that we can see plastics from space is concerning, as well as that there’s enough plastic out there that it’s changing the optical signal of the ocean, because that means it’s altering the light field in the ocean and potentially the way the ocean warms and cools.”

The color of the ocean reflects whatever is in its upper layer. That’s why it’s usually blue; water absorbs longer, redder wavelengths of light and scatters shorter, bluer wavelengths. Other elements, like sediment and microscopic organisms called phytoplankton, can affect the ocean’s hue, since sunlight interacts with those objects differently. However, there was a “gap” in the research on the effect of microplastics, says study co-author Dan Koestner, an ocean optics scientist at the University of Bergen in Norway, to Laura Paddison at CNN.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Did you know? Microplastics might be warming the atmosphere
In May, researchers reported that colorful bits of plastic swirling in the atmosphere might be reflecting sunlight and heating the surrounding air, contributing to climate change.

In previous lab experiments, Koestner had examined how lights and lasers scattered differently in ocean water that contained bits of plastic. Armed with that data, he and colleagues behind the new study examined three sets of satellite data showing one of the places in the ocean with the most plastic pollution: the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. Ocean currents trap piles of trash in this area, where they eventually break down into microplastics.

The team found that between 2002 and 2022, parts of the patch became 10 percent bluer and 2 to 4 percent greener, reports NBC News. The researchers then ran hundreds of computer simulations to find possible explanations for the change in color. When microplastics were excluded, only 3 percent of simulations produced the observed shift toward cyan. But including microplastics allowed 13 percent to mimic the real-world observations.
To confirm that microplastics are responsible for the ocean’s altered appearance, however, the researchers need to collect samples from the garbage patch.

“We’re still one step away from proving definitively that microplastics are causing the shift in color that we’re seeing,” says study co-author Shea Cheatham, also an ocean optics researcher at the University of Bergen, to Jackie Flynn Mogensen at Scientific American. “We just have to get in there [to the garbage patch] to verify.”

Richard Thompson, a marine biologist at the University of Plymouth in England who wasn’t involved in the research, tells CNN that the findings are important because detecting ocean microplastics is challenging given their size and tendency to get mixed in with phytoplankton and natural debris. “If we can detect change remotely from satellites it will be faster and less costly than counting debris piece by piece,” he says.

If the new study’s method can be verified, it can be used to identify other locations with microplastic accumulation, Koestner tells Scientific American. “That would mean that we have a target area for cleaning up.”

They carry their own brand of products, as well as some of the biggest names in the sex toy industry, plus lingerie, bondage gear, sexual wellness devices, and, of course, a wide variety of lube. articles.title: Ukraine, Russia agree to prisoner of war swap in UAE talks

paras.en: Nov. 11 (UPI) -- Ukrainian and Russian negotiators agreed to a "large-scale" prisoner swap Wednesday amid trilateral negotiations involving the United States in the United Arab Emirates, the head of Ukraine's intelligence service said.
The agreement came at the conclusion of two days of talks, the first aimed at ending the war in nine months.
Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, said negotiators were traveling back to their home countries to finalize the arrangements.

"Bringing our people home remains one of our top priorities," Umerov wrote in a post on X. "We are doing everything possible to ensure that every Ukrainian returns from captivity as soon as possible."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday praised a "revised approach" by U.S. mediators in the negotiations in Abu Dhabi.

Calling the talks "constructive and quite substantive," Zelensky said he was pleased with the different way U.S. negotiators were approaching the process and he was hopeful of more progress being made Wednesday.
"I see changes. I'm very happy with what I hear," he told reporters in Copenhagen.

Jared Kushner, who is representing the United States in negotiations along with U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, said Wednesday that he and Witkoff would meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday to finalize a prisoner swap agreed to at the talks, before traveling to Dublin to meet Zelensky.

Zelensky accused the Russian delegation of overstating the amount of territory Russian forces had captured, including a claim that Russia occupied half of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, saying it showed Putin was living in a "different reality" from everyone else.
"I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it's not true. What was good is that the American side confirmed the Ukrainian assessment of what is happening on the battlefield."
In a post on X after talks wrapped up for the day on Tuesday, Kushner expressed cautious optimism.
"We are encouraged by the constructive discussions today," he wrote.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was not at the talks, also expressed confidence, describing them as "very productive," but said the Europeans would at some point need to be part of the process "because they are part of solving this problem."

Kushner and Witkoff met with representatives from Britain, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission on the sidelines of the main talks in a bid to bridge the gulf in the positions of Moscow and European capitals, some of which are calling for an immediate, unconditional cease-fire before any negotiations can proceed.

However, three senior congressional Democrats accused Kushner and Witkoff on Wednesday of undermining Ukraine and the NATO alliance by entertaining Russian demands to renegotiate European security arrangements.

Reps. Gregory Meeks of New York and Adam Smith of Washington and Sen. Jack Reed of Rhode Island said Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, and Witkoff, a personal friend of the president, were pressuring Kyiv to surrender Ukrainian territory to Russia.

"Their parroting of Kremlin talking points on renegotiating European security and possibly pulling back from Eastern Europe is totally unacceptable to the continued viability of NATO and the national security of the United States," the Democrats said in a statement.

"Their Trumpian transactional approach, in which they are treating a nation's fight for survival like a real estate deal, threatens global stability. They and Trump are working for Putin, not for the benefit of the people of the United States."

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated Moscow's opposition to an immediate cease-fire, telling a news conference in Moscow on Tuesday that the only thing a truce would achieve would be to give Ukraine space to rebuild its military.

"European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said no discussions on security architecture would be held ahead of a sustainable cease-fire. This is the old logic again. By all means, it is necessary to buy time for their clients, the Kyiv regime, and use this time to restore to a certain extent, its military losses. We will not agree to it," he said.

articles.title: Police arrest teen for fatal shooting of 15-year-old Javits Frimpong

paras.en: Nov. 11 (UPI) -- Police in New York City on Wednesday morning arrested a teenager accused of the fatal Bronx shooting of 15-year-old Ghanaian national Javits Frimpong in late October.
The New York City Police Department identified the suspect as a 17-year-old boy. It said the teenager has been charged with murder.
"The NYPD will be relentless in our efforts to get dangerous people out of our communities, especially when it involves the murder of a 15-year-old boy," the NYPD said in a statement.
Frimpong was killed Oct. 29 while walking to school in the Bronx.

The NYPD said it had responded to a 911 call at about 9:30 a.m. that morning to find Frimpong in the vicinity of East 171st Street and Crotona Place suffering from a gunshot wound to the abdomen. The boy was transported to St. Barnabas Hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.
Frimpong had been living in the United States since Oct. 28, 2025, having moved to New York City to continue his education.
Police have not established a motive for the shooting.

Rev. Al Sharpton and attorney Ben Crump held a press conference Wednesday at the National Action Network's House of Justice in Harlem, alongside Frimpong's family and Ambassador Sam Kumah, Ghana's permanent representative to the United Nations, to demand justice for the slain child.
They spoke after being informed of the arrest.

"There is no justification for what happened to Javits and there is no way we will rest until people understand that we punish people in our community if they step out of line. We do not have a right to settle any disagreements we want in this manner," Sharpton said.
Frimpong's father, Thomas Frimpong, said he was "very, very happy" to know that an arrest had been made, but "still I need justice for my son."

Frimpong's mother, Doris Adyu-Gyamfi was in the United States on an emergency visa after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani appealed to President Donald Trump. Before the press conference, Crump said she was in the United States to bury her child.
"I need justice for my child. That's all. I have only one child," she said before breaking down in sobs.

articles.title: U.S. attorney demands Blumenthal preserve ballroom probe documents

paras.en: Nov. 12 (UPI) -- A U.S. attorney with the Justice Department demanded that Sen. Richard Blumenthal preserve all documents concerning his investigation into potential conflicts of interest stemming from the Trump administration's drive for private donations to construct the White House ballroom, accusing the Connecticut Democrat of threatening American citizens for associating with President Donald Trump.

"In recent weeks, you have threatened citizens for associating themselves with the president and other public officials. Yet, the 'freedom to engage in association for the advancement of beliefs and ideas is an inseparable aspect' of our Constitution and way of life," U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of the Southern District of Texas said in a Wednesday letter addressed to Blumenthal.

"It is also extraordinary for an elected official to intimidate citizens for engaging in philanthropic practices that will benefit our nation for generations. The American people are entitled to freely associate without elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action."
Trump's White House ballroom has faced criticism since it was announced in July 2025 and legal challenges since construction began later that year.

The president initially said it would cost $200 million and be paid for by private donors, but a contractor's internal estimate obtained by The Washington Post up the project's price tag at $600 million, with more than half expected to come from taxpayers.

Blumenthal, ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has been looking into waste, fraud and abuse connected to Trump administration construction projects in D.C., including the ballroom initiative.

On Oct. 21, Blumenthal announced letters had been sent to more than a dozen previously undisclosed White House ballroom donors made public in reporting by The Post. He asked them to name those who solicited the donations, say whether specific donation amounts were suggested and whether they were offered anonymity, as well as provide copies of any formal agreements and a list of all contacts donors or their representatives had with the White House or federal agencies.

"The American people are entitled to all the relevant facts about who is funding the most substantial construction project at the White House in recent history," Blumenthal wrote in one of the letters.
In his Wednesday letter to Blumenthal, Reitz gave the senator until 6 p.m. EST Nov. 18 to confirm that he has taken steps to preserve the materials.
"Failure to do so may result in sanctions, adverse-inference instructions or other penalties, and may carry significant legal consequences," the U.S. attorney said.
Blumenthal responded to Reitz in a letter: "I will not be intimidated."

"I will work on behalf of the American people to vigorously pursue investigations into this administration's persistent misuse of taxpayer dollars and any corporate entity that has enabled their boundless corruption," he said in a statement.
"The public deserves to know the terms under which dozens of American companies were persuaded to donate millions of dollars to the president's vanity projects."

The Trump administration has repeatedly used the powers of the executive branch, including the Justice Department, to impose punitive measures and launch investigations and criminal proceedings against the president's perceived opponents.

The letter to Blumenthal follows a letter from White House counsel Will Scharf to Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., ranking member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, warning that Democratic investigations in to Trump, his family and other Republican allies could constitute criminal conduct.
Garcia responded Wednesday by accusing the White House of threatening to infringe upon the committee's constitutionally protected right to conduct congressional oversight.
"It appears Donald Trump has something to hide," Garcia said in a statement.

The legal pressure is being applied to the Democrats after they won control of both the House and the Senate in last week's midterm elections, which had increasingly occupied Trump's attention in the preceding months, having warned GOP lawmakers that if they lost control of Congress, impeachment and investigations would follow.
"The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia continued.

"The Trump administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the president's lawyers."

articles.title: Young Thug and Birdman Dismissed From Lawsuit Over 2015 Lil Wayne Tour Bus Shooting
articles.author: Rachel Scharf

paras.en: After a decade of litigation, Young Thug and Birdman have triumphed over legal claims that sought to hold them liable for a shooting on Lil Wayne’s tour bus in Atlanta.

Two Georgia court orders on Tuesday (Nov. 10), obtained by Billboard, dismissed Thug (Jeffrey Williams) and Birdman (Bryan Williams) from the lawsuit filed back in 2016 by Wayne’s former tour bus driver, Alvin Lewis. The driver still has civil claims for emotional damages pending against two other men over the 2015 shooting, a drive-by that occurred on the I-285 freeway after Wayne performed at The Compound club in Atlanta.

A man named Jimmy Winfrey (also known as Peewee Roscoe) pled guilty to the shooting in 2015, though that admission was wiped on appeal after it was found to be involuntary. Winfrey separately pled guilty in 2024 as part of the sweeping YSL racketeering prosecution, in which the Wayne tour bus incident was cited as one of several violent acts supposedly connected to Thug’s Atlanta label. Thug ultimately went free in that criminal case after a dramatic legal saga.

In the civil case, Lewis alleged that Winfrey was working at the direction of both Thug and Birdman when he shot at Wayne’s tour bus. Both rappers say they had nothing to do with the shooting. Judge Eric A. Brewton sided with the duo on Tuesday, saying there’s “no evidence of an employment relationship” between Winfrey and either YSL or Birdman’s Cash Money Records.

The lawsuit claimed that Winfrey was Thug’s tour manager in 2015, but Judge Brewton said this is unsupported by any evidence. As for Birdman, the judge said there was nothing but “pure speculation and conjecture” in Lewis’ theory that the Cash Money boss orchestrated the shooting to get back at Wayne for suing his label that year.

Lewis obtained evidence showing a series of calls placed in 2015 between Winfrey’s phone and Birdman’s phone, including on the night of the shooting. Judge Brewton said this did not move the needle, however, since he couldn’t tell “who made what calls, whether any calls were picked up and by whom, whether any conversation was had, or the content of any conversation.”

The judge thus threw out all claims against Thug, YSL, Birdman and Cash Money. Lewis’ attorney, Jeff Gewirtz, told Billboard on Wednesday (Nov. 11) that they plan to appeal the decision. Reps for Thug and Birdman did not return requests for comment.

Lewis still has claims against Winfrey and another man named Arnold Martinez, known as YSL Duke, who was also wrapped up in the YSL gang prosecution. A court conference to discuss potential trial logistics is scheduled for February.

articles.title: Ebro & Peter Rosenberg Aren’t Buying Ye’s ‘Comeback’ Narrative After Antisemitism: ‘It’s All Marketing’
articles.author: Michael Saponara

paras.en: Ye (formerly Kanye West) has been selling out stadiums across the globe with spot tour dates throughout 2026, most recently packing more than 83,000 fans into AT&T Stadium in Dallas for a show over the weekend.

Ebro Darden and Peter Rosenberg debated the merits of West’s touring in 2026 on Monday’s (Nov. 9) episode of The Ebro Laura Rosenberg Show, and the media personalities aren’t buying the comeback narrative tied to Ye following his antisemitic remarks and controversial antics in years past.

Prior to the Ye talk, the co-hosts discussed Macklemore’s Free Palestine Tour and his claims that arenas across the U.S. were attempting to censor him by not allowing him to perform due to his political beliefs.

“The venues can say whatever the f— they want to do. … They can do this, and say, ‘Hey, we don’t want you here,'” Ebro said. “My suggestion always in these sort of things is you go get a smaller venue and you block out multiple nights and you do a residency-style thing.”
That led into Peter Rosenberg bringing up Ye having back-to-back sold-out shows in Houston and Dallas earlier this month. “Everyone’s celebrating,” Rosenberg quipped.

“Everybody was hitting me talking about how record-breaking it was,” Ebro replied. “And I was like, ‘Guys, I’ve been involved in concerts before. I know how to make the stage setup so you can get more people in the building and make it look like you got more numbers.’ He still sold the tickets.”

Rosenberg believes “people are enjoying it extra” when it comes to West’s return to performing in stadiums “because now it has the extra sauce of the perceived comeback thing too.” He added: “People love a comeback story. Like, he was down bad, guys. He was down to his last billion.”

Ebro explained that as a society, “We’re all victims of marketing. It’s all marketing.” Rosenberg questioned West’s acts of contrition amid his comeback trail, which included taking out a full-page ad in The Wall Street Journal to apologize to the Jewish and Black communities, and also meeting with a rabbi.
Rosenberg and Ebro’s comments went viral on social media, and Rosenberg addressed the Ye fans in his mentions on X. “Kanye fans were hip hop fans,” he claimed. “Ye fans are just weirdos.”

West will wrap up his Stateside touring with his final U.S. show of 2026 on Nov. 21 at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona. He made North American stops throughout the year in Los Angeles, Tampa Bay, San Antonio, Chicago, New Orleans, Houston and Dallas.
On the music front, Ye released his Bully album in March, which debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200.
Watch the full Ebro Laura Rosenberg Show below. Talk about Ye takes place shortly after the hour mark.

articles.title: Anyma Will Return to the Great Pyramids of Giza In 2027
articles.author: Lars Brandle

paras.en: Anyma will return next spring to the Great Pyramids of Giza, Egypt, the setting of his record-setting shows in 2025. Only this time he’s bringing with him one of the great wonders of the electronic music world — Jean-Michel Jarre.

The Italian-American producer and DJ (real name: Matteo Milleri) will stage two spectacular electronic performances at the Pyramids, titled ÆDEN MILLENNIUM, on March 19 and 26, 2027. It’s a touch of history repeating for Anyma, who last October used the canvas of the Pyramids for two sold-out shows, which drew fans from 92 countries, reps say.

“I’ve been fortunate enough to bring my show to some incredible venues around the world in the past few years, but the two-part show at the Pyramids of Giza has been by far one of the most memorable,” he explains in a statement.

“I’m working on a new, entirely unique production for our return in 2027, especially paying tribute to the magnitude of the area’s beauty and history,” he continues. “I can’t wait to share ÆDEN MILLENNIUM with you in Egypt next year.”

Jarre will share the stage for both dates, for what will mark the French electronic music pioneer’s own return to Giza after ringing in the Millennium with his 12-hour production, The Twelve Dreams Of The Sun.

“Delighted to accept Anyma’s invitation to join forces,” Jarre remarks. “When I welcomed the new Millennium at the Great Pyramids of Egypt, my ambition was to create a dialogue between this ancient setting and the future through music, light and technology. It’s exciting to return with Anyma, who shares that same spirit of exploration, and imagine a new chapter together.”
Jarre, now aged 78, is 22 albums deep in a career that places him at the head of the table for electronic music’s greatest and most influential artists.

Among his masterpieces is debut Oxygene, which this year celebrates its 50th anniversary. To celebrate its milestone, Jarre embarked on a pan-European run of summer concerts, including a performance at Amnesia Ibiza, for the club’s own half-century celebrations, and he appeared as special guest of honor at the 30th edition of Amsterdam Dance Event in October, where he presented the sold-out opening concert, “Oxygene & Beyond: A Sonic Journey Celebrating 30 Years of ADE.”

Born in Lyon, France, Jarre has clocked up career album sales north of 85 million, and was awarded the Commander of the Légion d’Honneur in 2021, France’s highest order of merit. President Emmanuel Macron was on hand for the presentation.

He’s readying the release of a special edition of Oxygene on Nov. 20 through an expanded new partnership with BMG, and the U.S. publication of Machines: A History Of Electronic Music on Nov. 24 via Thames & Hudson.

Anyma launched his all-new live show ÆDEN at his headline set at Coachella 2026, and has since presented it across the globe, including a performance to 65,000 people in Mexico City, and at China’s largest ever electronic headline concert, May 2 in Shanghai.
Tickets for ÆDEN MILLENNIUM will be available on artist presale from Nov. 18 at 2pm GMT (9am ET), with general sale from Nov. 19 at 2pm GMT. More acts for both dates will be announced in due course.

articles.title: ‘South Park’ Gives Its Fan-Favorite Couple Their Own ‘Heated Rivalry’
articles.author: Kevin Dolak

paras.en: In a sweet blend of fan service and meta-commentary on American politics, South Park brought back Tweek and Craig (aka Creek), two fan-favorite supporting players who haven’t had the spotlight on Comedy Central’s long-running animated hit in years, for “We Be Clubbin’,” the penultimate episode of season 29. The series has been parodying the trends and idiosyncrasies of modern life for decades, and this week’s targets are club sports, performative parenting and Heated Rivalry.

The episode opens with a school assembly led by Mr. Garrison, who nods to the episode’s subtle political commentary by mentioning the blue wave that cost Republicans their congressional majorities last week. He then introduces PC Principal, who seems to have dropped his MAGA vibe for the pseudo-liberal party-guy vibe we know and love, celebrating the Democrats’ victory with a shout of “We’re back.” Before PC Principal’s lengthy dance routine, Garrison, in another bit of meta comedy, gives a quick nod to this season’s lack of President Donald Trump, who was a central player in the show’s prior two seasons.

paras.en: “I know you’ve all heard about the midterms and the severe beating our president took,” he announces. “And of course we could just go on and on and make a bunch of jokes about him, but it’s no fun punching down on a helpless loser.”

Garrison’s brief mention of gay students at South America Elementary reminds Eric Cartman, the tireless romantic, that it’s Tweek and Craig’s anniversary. Tweek has noticed too. When he brings it up with his frequently absent boyfriend and gets an utter lack of enthusiasm (or recollection), he hatches a plan to get more Craig time: He convinces his parents to let him try out for youth club sports, an endeavor that soon eats up all of the boy’s and his parents’ time and money.
Tweek’s tryout for club sports, the all-consuming and costly circuit of nonspecific sporting extracurriculars, is the first red flag that he and his parents are being swindled.

“School sports are fine, but they only take a child so far. That’s why it’s great to hear you might want to join club sports,” the portly shyster representing Sacks, formerly Cumhammer, tells the Tweaks. “Now, have you got that $26 tryout fee?”

The fees only snowball for the Tweak family as the big, bossy Sacks rep sends them to Boulder, Fort Collins and all around the state for vague sporting events, with growing charges for parking, for spectating and, of course, for the bar tab at each event, where drafts on tap go for $14. The bar is where club sports parents unload on one another about how “exhausting” it is to be club sports parents, though they could never let their precious kids be “left behind,” whatever that actually means.

“Oh, you’re so lucky!” one mother gushes. “You only have one kid. We spent the week getting up at two in the morning to get our three kids to 50 different cities and stay in nine hotel rooms at the same time!”

Meanwhile, on courts across Colorado, our over-caffeinated friend is stuck in the lower league, away from his beloved Craig. Tweek grows more and more frustrated about not seeing him, but there’s no time to dwell, because it’s off with his parents again. Only when the unnamed club sports swindler realizes that Tweek and Craig are a gay couple are both boosted to the Triple-A league together, and the inevitable nods to the hit HBO Max series Heated Rivalry arrive. Naturally, this is far worse for Tweek and Craig, since it eats up all of their time (all of it). But it’s a glow-up for Tweek’s parents in the spectators’ bar, where they now get to lord it over everyone in the backhanded bragging game with the busiest schedule of all.

He’s spending at least some time with Craig amid their packed club sports schedules, though it’s starting to drive the eternally stoic Craig a bit batty. Tweek, who delivers an A+ Craig impression here, asks him why he needs to fill his life with club sports and gets the Sacks shyster’s spiel parroted back at him: You’ll be left behind, you won’t get into college and so on. Suddenly, amid a Tweek-style freak-out (complete with hat-pulling), it hits Craig: He forgot their anniversary.

articles.title: Compassion and Bureaucracy Clash in ‘A Job Well Done,’ Which Explores Immigration Through Social Workers’ Eyes
articles.author: Georg Szalai

paras.en: What do you do when the only way to help someone is to break the rules and the law? This clash between compassion and solidarity on the one side and the legal framework on the other is at the heart of A Job Well Done (Un travail exemplaire), the new feature blending fiction and documentary from Swiss writer-director Fred Baillif, which dives into the complexities and moral ambiguity that social workers face.

In his work, the former national basketball player and prison educator draws on his background in social work to make films that are rooted in real life and explore contradictions that people working on the tricky frontlines of social services. He previously put a spotlight on street work in Tapis rouge and life in a group home in The Fam (La Mif).

In A Job Well Done, Baillif takes us inside a double-decker bus in Geneva, where social workers welcome migrants who are looking for help, a shelter, or simply someone to talk to. On this frontline of Switzerland’s asylum system, the desire to help refugees means navigating an increasingly Kafkaesque bureaucracy.

“Behind every file, a life is told: a young woman in conflict with her family, an asylum seeker facing deportation, homeless people, a woman trying to escape violence,” reads a synopsis on the PÖFF website. “The team looks for solutions, negotiates, insists. But places are scarce, procedures run their course, and institutional responses collide with the urgency of the situations. Among colleagues, convictions clash: keep within the framework to preserve the welcome, or step outside it rather than abandon someone?”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The film will have its world premiere on Nov. 14 in the Official Selection Competition at the the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia. Watch a trailer here.
“What interests me is the moment when a profession collides with bureaucracy without offering real alternatives,” says Baillif. “I want the viewer to experience this conflict.”

A Job Well Done grew out of immersions at AMIC, the Association of Intercultural Mediators, and at the migration and integration center Roseraie in Geneva. Baillif met professionals and the people they support. Through interviews and improvisation workshops, he developed the situations, characters and words from which the screenplay was built with Joanne Giger. The cast brings together professional actors and non-professional performers who know social work or have experience with migration. Through improvisation, the performers find their own words and reactions within a dramaturgical framework.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The cast of the Alva Film production, co-produced by Fresh Prod and RTS Radio Télévision Suisse, features Sewit Abadi, Sabbel Ceesay, Rebecca Baillif, Claudia Grob and Selam Tesfu.
Baillif talked to THR about his filmmaking process and the urgency of A Job Well Done.
Can you explain your filmmaking process and how it has fictional and real-life elements a bit?

It’s a very specific way of working. It’s not only based on what I have experienced. It’s more based on what my characters not only have experienced, but, especially in this movie, also how they feel and the way they behave in real life. So the whole work with them is to help them just be themselves as much as they can during the shoot.

When we shoot the movie, I have a script. But the script and what’s inside every scene is always very flexible because, for me, the main idea is that they know better. They are the experts for those things because that’s what they actually do in their real life. They are social workers. They work with immigrants in their everyday life.
Do you have any examples of how actors may surprise you with their input?

There is a scene in the film about sexual mutilation, and in the script, we had the idea that [the social worker] would be very angry. That was our idea because it makes us very angry, us as white people from here.
But when we shot the scene, Sewit, our actress, told me, “No, I’m not going to be angry. I’m going to be very careful and very empathetic.” That’s an example of how I work.
I guess that also allows you to avoid the white savior lens that could come into play?

They are the experts, so I’m just going to listen to them. And coming from documentary, it’s just obvious to me that I’m not the, as you said, white savior explaining to the world what immigration is and what it is to work with immigrants. This system of directing, this concept I have developed through my films, for me is now just the way I work. I don’t think I would be able to work another way.
Was any scene in A Job Well Done particularly difficult to shoot for you or the cast?

I wanted my wife Rebecca to be in the film because she also works as a social worker. We did a scene where she’s telling her boss that she’s actually being racist in a way. This scene was very difficult for her because she wouldn’t scream, especially at an elderly person. With her African background, she respects older people a lot. So it was hard for her to do the scene, but she really did it with a lot of authenticity. It feels so real that we really enjoyed it.
The film feels really timely and addresses a topic that is causing much debate around the globe. Are there any political angles you were particularly interested in?

The idea was to talk about how we in the Western world see the “useful” and the “useless” migrants, especially in Geneva, where we have a lot of international organizations and global companies. They are big companies that come there and hire people. Those expats are the good migrants that we want, and it’s easy for them to get papers and work because we need them. And the others, we don’t need because they may not have the same background. So for me, it’s absolutely unfair.

But the focus was on the social workers, because I wanted to do something about immigration, but I didn’t want to have another movie focusing on an immigrant. Through real social workers, we can see the impact that immigration has on us who have to deal with those laws that are very restrictive.

And, of course, I also wanted to talk about how if you don’t follow the rules, then you can become an outlaw yourself. There are many examples of how you cannot follow the rules. It’s impossible when you work with people every day, and they have needs, and you have to help them. It’s impossible to just follow the rules – that is what I wanted to say because that’s what they told me about their work.

articles.title: The Hottest New Tables in Hollywood During AFM
articles.author: Melinda Sheckells

paras.en: At the Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills, chef Edo Baldi gives the steakhouse an Italian accent, cooking beef and wagyu over an olive wood-fired grill. Don’t let the steaks distract from sweet corn tortellini with mascarpone and truffle butter, or the pancake soufflé for two. Terracotta tones and olive trees warm the restaurant. For casual meet-ups, Bar Baldi pairs thin-crust pizza with beverage director Jim Kearns’ limoncello-laced spritz.

Moving from Santa Monica into the former Lumière space, chef Jeremy Fox’s Birdie G’s brings its family-inspired cooking directly to Century City. Matzo ball soup, the Pickle Chick cutlet and rose petal pie join koji-aged steaks, handmade pastas and California vegetables. EDG’s design draws on midcentury supper clubs, with banquettes and expanded patio seating. The planned breakfast-through-dinner format covers the working day; martinis and Manhattans take care of happy hour and beyond.
267 N. Canon Drive, Suite A7, Beverly Hills

The former Palm steakhouse has a new cast of characters: a boar sculpture, greyhound statues and snake door handles. Quality Branded’s Bad Roman fills green velvet banquettes with diners sharing garlic babka and pepperoni cups with ranch. Chefs Craig Koketsu and Clint Ives oversee filet mignon topped with a cacio e pepe raviolo and lemon-shaped cheesecake. Order a pepperoncini martini or flaming Vesuvius Bowl. Shots arrive attached to miniature Italian cars.

Dinner can turn into karaoke at Little Luck, The h.wood Group’s Japanese izakaya on the Sunset Strip. Two private dining rooms come equipped for singing, while roughly 4,000 records supply the soundtrack. Chef Erik Idos, an L.A. native whose Nobu years took him to Hong Kong, returns with sashimi, nigiri, skewers and charcoal-grilled meats and seafood for sharing. Dark woods, amber lighting and lantern-like fixtures make Kevin Lee’s cocktails look as incredible as they taste.

For a meeting that starts with “just one glass,” Wally’s Century Plaza offers more than 50 possibilities. The new concept directly in front of the Fairmont pairs wines by the glass with a full cocktail program and a California-French menu that also draws on Wally’s signatures.
10200 Constellation Blvd., Suite 225, Los Angeles

Follow the fire to KYU, the Miami-born restaurant making its California debut at Century Plaza Promenade on Nov. 9. Roasted cauliflower, Korean fried chicken, tuna crispy rice and wood-fired short rib anchor the menu, with new dishes developed for Los Angeles. An open kitchen sits at the center of the more than 6,000-square-foot space, while a curved facade faces the plaza’s fountain.

articles.title: The world's super-rich are piling into alternative investments. Here's why

paras.en: The world's wealthiest investors are increasingly looking beyond stocks and bonds, pouring money into hedge funds, private equity and infrastructure assets, as market volatility and fears about stubborn inflation spur diversification.
From Asian billionaires to global family offices, alternative investments are becoming a bigger part of portfolios once dominated by traditional assets, said industry watchers

JPMorgan Asset Management's private wealth alternative assets in Asia-Pacific surged 40% over the past 12 months, according to Dan Watkins, the firm's regional chief executive officer, underscoring the growing appetite among high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients.
"So you really have this huge appetite for alternative exposure happening in that ultra-high-net-worth, high-net-worth category," Watkins said recently at a media summit in Singapore.

The shift comes as investors grapple with increasingly concentrated equity markets, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns that stocks and bonds may not provide the same protection against market downturns as they once did, experts said.
"We are seeing a sharp increase in planned asset allocation to alternatives among the family offices we speak to," said John Woods, chief investment officer for Asia at Lombard Odier.

Alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios, surpassing traditional assets for the first time, according to BNY Wealth. Traditional assets accounted for 41% of allocations, the report found.

Wealthy investors are seeking diversification, income and access to investments outside listed markets, and concerns over elevated valuations, tight credit spreads and the growing correlation between stocks and bonds have accelerated the trend, Woods added.
Hedge funds are emerging as a favored option among wealthy investors seeking protection against market swings, particularly as traditional diversification strategies face growing challenges.

Olaolu Aganga, head of portfolio construction and analytics at Citi Wealth, said hedge funds have attracted the strongest recent interest among qualified clients, who are seeking returns less dependent on the direction of equity markets.

Private credit is another area drawing interest, offering investors contractual income streams, while some hedge fund strategies seek to profit from differences in performance between companies rather than relying on broad market rallies, said Woods.
Citi's 2026 survey of 351 family offices found that inflation was their biggest concern, followed by interest rates, financial system stability and market volatility.

Wealthy families are increasingly seeking investments that can generate income and help preserve purchasing power amid persistent inflation and interest-rate uncertainty, while diversifying portfolios against market volatility, according to Aganga.

The Citi survey, however, also showed public equities recorded the strongest net increase in allocations, suggesting wealthy investors are adding alternatives rather than abandoning traditional markets. "This is not a wholesale rotation away from public markets," Woods said.
Infrastructure has emerged as another major beneficiary of the shift, with the artificial intelligence boom creating enormous demand for data centers, electricity networks and digital connectivity.

Thomas Roland Guyot, head of private markets investment specialists for Southeast Asia at UBS Unified Global Alternatives, said investors are increasingly targeting assets that support AI, electrification and energy security.
Such investments potentially offer a combination of long-term growth and relatively predictable cash flows, particularly where revenues are supported by essential demand or long-term contracts.

Investor appetite is already showing up in fund flows. Net inflows into open-ended infrastructure funds rose 30% year on year in the 12 months through the first quarter of 2026, according to PitchBook data cited by UBS.

Private equity remains a cornerstone of wealthy investors' alternative portfolios, although they are becoming more selective. Family offices are increasingly favoring direct investments in companies, co-investments alongside private equity managers and purchases of existing fund stakes on the secondary market, rather than relying solely on traditional pooled funds, according to Citi Wealth's Aganga.
Such approaches can give investors greater control over their investments or opportunities to acquire assets at discounts, said Lombard Odier's Woods.

The broader shift is also being facilitated by the growth of evergreen and semi-liquid funds, which have lowered minimum investment thresholds and reduced some administrative hurdles associated with traditional private-market funds, Woods added.
Investing into alternative assets does not come without risks, even as mitigating those is driving flows.

Private investments can lock up capital for years, while valuations may be slow to reflect deteriorating market conditions. Even funds marketed as semi-liquid can restrict withdrawals when redemption requests surge.
"Improved access does not equal liquidity," JPMorgan's Watkins said.

Citi's Aganga also warned that performance can vary significantly between managers, while private assets may appear less volatile than they actually are because valuations are updated less frequently.

Investors must also guard against unintended concentration. A portfolio holding data centers through real estate, infrastructure and private equity funds may appear diversified while remaining heavily exposed to the same AI investment cycle, UBS' Guyot said.

For now, the flow of capital into alternative assets shows their increasing appeal among the rich, though not at the expense of traditional investment, with Woods pointing out that much of the new investment is being funded by fresh capital and excess cash rather than large-scale sales of stocks and bonds.

articles.title: Nvidia board meeting to decide CEO Jensen Huang’s fate stretches into evening

paras.en: Nvidia's board is meeting to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang, CNBC confirmed late Wednesday, following reports of two extramarital affairs — one with an employee and another with an alleged Chinese spy.

Shares of Nvidia fell more than 9% in post-market trading after The Wall Street Journal first reported that the board was preparing to force out Huang. That news landed minutes after The New York Times reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with Nvidia's vice president of health care.

The alleged relationship, according to the Times story, was with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Powell's bio on the Nvidia website says she's "responsible for the company's worldwide healthcare business, including hardware and software platforms for accelerated computing, AI, and visualization that power the ecosystem of medical imaging, life sciences, drug discovery, and healthcare analytics."
Huang and Powell were reportedly captured on camera being affectionate with one another at a hotel in San Jose, California in March, according to the Times.
Nvidia and Powell didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

The report comes days after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman who is believed by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, according to The Financial Times, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported.
Nvidia's board of directors has opened an independent investigation and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to look into the spying allegations.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message to Nvidia staff on Sunday. "I am deeply sorry."

Most of Huang's Nvidia shares are co-owned with his wife, Lori Huang, and are held in trusts. About 800 million shares are held by those trusts. Huang holds about 70 million shares on his own and has limited economic control over the company.

Rumors of an affair between Huang and Powell have circulated for years, in part because Powell lacks a background in health or science, according to a former employee who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter.

Healthcare is a smaller business at Nvidia. The company makes chips for medical devices and MRI machines, but they are a minor in comparison to the revenue generated from its advanced AI systems and graphics processing units, or GPUs. In recent appearances, including at the company's annual GTC conference, Powell has spoken about how Nvidia's AI technology can help accelerate drug discovery, assist providers and improve clinical efficiency. Powell has been leading the group since 2017.

Nvidia's stock was down 7% this week prior to the after-hours drop on Wednesday and is on pace for its sixth straight weekly slide, reflecting broad concern on the sustainability of the artificial intelligence buildout. The AI infrastructure trade was hit particularly hard last week after the midterm elections, as Democrats won sweeping majorities in both houses of Congress, and dozens of ballot measures past that could make building data centers more difficult.

Huang has become synonymous with the AI industry, and he is often referred to by his first name ,"Jensen," by customers and rivals. Nvidia has been one of the primary beneficiaries of the AI boom since its chips are used to train models and run large AI workloads.
—CNBC's Lora Kolodny and Kif Leswing contributed to this report

articles.title: Treasury yields edge higher as investors await fresh inflation and housing data

paras.en: U.S. Treasury yields edged higher Thursday as bond trading resumed after the Veterans Day closure and investors looked ahead to fresh inflation and housing data for clues about the economy and the Federal Reserve's next move.
The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note — the benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was up 2 basis points at 5.0100%.

The 2-year Treasury note yield, which is more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was 5 basis points higher at 4.7800%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury note yield — which often moves on geopolitical developments — was steady at 5.3503%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
The rise in yields comes as traders await more domestic data releases this week for fresh insights into the U.S. economic picture.
On Friday, the latest monthly producer price inflation print, which tracks wholesale inflation, is expected to show a 0.4% rise in October, down from the 1.3% surge in September.

Before that, investors are also looking out for October's home sales report from the National Association of Realtors, due later Thursday. Existing home sales rose by 1.5% in September to 3.99 million, up from a two-year low the previous month, and are expected to reach 4 million last month, according to Trading Economics estimates.

Oil prices were broadly flat in early trading, as Middle East negotiations remain deadlocked. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were up less than 0.1% at $86.59 a barrel, while Brent crude rose 0.17% to $92.92.

articles.title: What an exceptionally powerful El Niño could mean for hurricanes, drought and flooding

paras.en: Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
You’ve probably heard by now, possibly even on this very podcast, that this year’s El Niño is on track to be one of the strongest ever recorded. But what does that mean for our weather forecasts?
Scientific American’s senior editor for Earth and environment Andrea Thompson is here to demystify this atmospheric phenomenon.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Thanks so much for coming on to chat with us.
Feltman: So we’ve talked, briefly, about this year’s El Niño in a couple other episodes. But let’s start with the basics just to refresh our listeners’ memories. What exactly is El Niño?

Thompson: Right. So it’s this, sort of, cyclical climate phenomenon. Its epicenter is in the tropical Pacific Ocean. And so basically in, sort of, normal times or on average, trade winds blow from east to west and across the tropical Pacific, and that, sort of, piles warm water up around Indonesia.

But in El Niño times, those winds weaken or can even reverse, and that means all of that warm water, sort of, sloshes back over toward the eastern tropical Pacific. And that can have really big impacts because that heat isn’t just limited to the ocean; it’s releasing out into the atmosphere. And that changes where clouds and storms form, which has, sort of, this domino effect in the atmosphere that can change major weather circulation patterns.

And, for example, it tends to quash hurricane activity in the Atlantic because you get a lot of what we call wind shear, so sort of cross-cutting winds, whereas in the Pacific Ocean, it tends to ramp up hurricane activity, which we’ve seen both of those play out over this hurricane season with really not a lot happening in the Atlantic and then whole bunch of flurry of storms in the Pacific.

And this particular El Niño is really, really strong; so the, the warm waters in the Eastern Pacific right now are just record-breakingly hot in terms of basically any El Niño we’ve seen in our lifetimes.

Feltman: Well and we’ve heard a lot about how this year’s El Niño is so intense. So I guess, a few questions there that we can tackle one at a time. How intense is it? How do we know? And then: What kinds of impacts are we gonna see because of that? So let’s start with just, you know, what do we mean by saying this is such a powerful El Niño, and how does it compare to previous years?

Thompson: Right. So we mainly measure that based on the sea surface temperatures in a specific part of the Pacific Ocean. And we, sort of, monitor what those temperatures are doing. If they reach a certain threshold, that’s when we say, “We’re in an El Niño,” and then if they get, you know, really high, then you could say, “This is a very strong El Niño.”

And these have been breaking records since September. I talk to climate scientists who are, kind of, just aghast at how strong this one is. Right now, temperatures in the, sort of, core part of the Pacific where we monitor El Niño are about 3.5 degrees Celsius above normal. That is astounding. They could reach four degrees Celsius above normal, when this event, sort of, peaks, which typically happens in the November-December timeframe for El Niños. And those just, sort of, absolutely smash any heat records we have, at least with direct temperature measurements. Those go back to, into the 19th century, and the, sort of, the record we have was set by an El Niño in 1877.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: We can also estimate sea surface temperatures going further back than, you know, direct temperature measurements based on things like tree growth rings, coral growth rings, and those tree rings tell us how El Niño–related precipitation changes happened. And then coral growth rings are actually a little bit more direct. How the coral grows is related to sea surface temperatures. And so those we can build out an estimate going back to around the year 1100, and this would probably set records even going back that far. So this is a truly astounding event.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Feltman: Wow. And do we know why this is happening?

Thompson: It can be hard to say. So, you know, El Niño and especially really big El Niños are still relatively rare events, and so you don’t quite have enough data to really be able to piece out why they happen when they happen. Anytime data is rare, it’s very hard to find a trend. There is some new research that indicates that climate change may be pushing us more toward these really strong El Niños. That’s based also in coral records. So it could be that we’re seeing more of these in part because of climate change.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But some of it’s also probably just the chaos of the Earth’s system that, you know, sometimes you’re gonna get one, and sometimes you aren’t. And of course, there’s a baseline warming of the world’s oceans that’s feeding into this a little bit, but even, sort of, subtracting that from the ocean temperatures, this El Niño is still outstanding.

Feltman: Right. Well, and so segueing into the impacts we can expect, you know, even though we can’t necessarily pin this on climate change, the fact that climate change is happening and global temperatures are already warmer and weather is already weirder probably means that a really extreme El Niño is maybe more worrying than it would’ve been a couple decades ago. Would you say that that’s correct?

Thompson: Definitely can, because for an example, El Niño tends to bring drought conditions to the Amazon. And the Amazon is already in a weakened state, both in part because of a previous strong El Niño that caused drought and contributed to wildfires as well as climate change acting on that and exacerbating those droughts. And then other, of course, land-use change happening in parts of the Amazon. So you don’t just have the effects of this El Niño, you have all those other things playing in.

And then we have various what are called teleconnections in scientific parlance, where El Niño has certain effects in certain places. And generally these are more robust when you have a very strong El Niño just because you have more input into the system from the El Niño. So, you know, you have the effects on hurricanes in the Atlantic and the Pacific, where we’ve seen almost no hurricane activity in the Atlantic this year and a flurry of storms especially around Hawaii and the Pacific. You’ve also seen a major drought and wildfires in Indonesia. That is a hallmark of El Niños.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And generally, the closer places are to where El Niño is, sort of, happening, the stronger the impacts are, which makes sense. But they can reach really far afield too, so you know, there are teleconnections in Africa. You tend to have more rainfall and flooding in the Horn of Africa but less rainfall and drought in, sort of, South Africa. And it’s going to be particularly interesting to watch this winter.

So, you know, with the climate being warmer than it was in the past, you know, it’s unclear how much of the precipitation from these storms may fall as rain instead of snow when what you want in the West is snow because that snowpack is, sort of, what gives you the water that lasts you through spring, summer and fall.

These storms also bring a lot of coastal waves, we already have exceptionally high sea levels off the coast of California right now ’cause it’s very warm there, too, and we have these, sort of, pulses of warm water that can come up from the main El Niño region called Kelvin waves, which I know we talked about before. And so all of that together could mean we have a lot of major coastal flooding in California this winter.
Feltman: Right. So how much do we know about how long the El Niño is gonna last?

Thompson: So we have a pretty good understanding of, sort of, the cadence of El Niño. It tends to always peak in the November/December/January timeframe. This one has ramped up a lot faster than ones we’ve seen in the past, so it got warm very quickly.

It’s a little unclear exactly how high it’s going to peak, and that might determine how long temperatures stay really elevated. If it peaks higher, it may take longer for them to come down. After it peaks, it’ll, sort of, slowly come down through the winter.

But winter is typically the time where we see the biggest impacts, at least in the Northern Hemisphere, in the U.S. It’s gonna last several more months. Eventually it will, sort of, exhaust itself, and ocean temperatures will get back to, sort of, more typical levels, and then we’ll be in what’s called, sort of, neutral conditions.

But the heat of an El Niño in the atmosphere always lags the heat in the ocean, the heat in the ocean peaks November/December-ish. Heat in the atmosphere follows a few months behind. So we’re going to see global temperatures stay elevated for longer. Right now it’s a little unclear if 2026 is going to be the hottest year on record. Very well could be. It’s definitely going to be up there, which is pretty remarkable because we started this year in, sort of, a weak La Niña state, so ...
Feltman: Which brings temperatures down?

Thompson: Down, yeah. So no one was expecting that this was going to be a contender. It will definitely be 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial this year, which would be the second year that’s ever happened after 2024.

[The year] 2027 [is] almost certainly going to be the warmest year on record because of that heat lag. And it will also be warmer than 1.5 C. And one thing I’ve talked to with some scientists is the question of: Do we come back down from that, or are we, sort of, at 1.5 C from now on? Now, that still wouldn’t technically breach the climate agreement ’cause that’s considered an average over many, many years, but it’s possible.

Now, if we swing over to La Niña, maybe we come back down below 1.5 C above preindustrial. It’s a little hard to tell. But, you know, this is definitely not going in the direction we want things to go in, for sure

Feltman: Yeah. I remember years ago, at this point, an expert I talked to said, you know, “We’re on an escalator. El Niño is us getting up on our tippy-toes, and La Niña is us ducking down, but the escalator keeps going up.” And that has really stuck with me all these years.

Thompson: Right. Yeah, and typically, sort of, El Niño’s temperature effects on the globe are temporary. Eventually that heat is radiated back to space. But what a couple climate scientists pointed out to me is that the same, sort of, feedbacks that happen with climate change, where you have sea ice melts or permafrost thawings that can, sort of, exacerbate it, those are sort of agnostic to where that additional heat comes from. So if you have more heat coming from El Niño, those might also ramp up those feedbacks and, sort of, effectively lock some of the El Niño heat into the system instead of it just being temporary.
