paras.en: “ESPA helped redefine access to space by enabling additional payloads to share a launch with primary missions. Its impact continues across commercial, government, and military space—and its story reflects the value of enduring collaboration between Air Force Research Lab (AFRL) and industry partners such as Moog,” said Dr. Darren Raspa, chief historian, AFRL Space and Directed Energy Systems.

Over the past 25 years, the ESPA family has evolved into a versatile, modular platform supporting varied payload sizes and interface configurations. ESPA-derived designs have also served as the structural foundation for spacecraft buses. Today, the platform continues to support mission planning for NASA, the U.S. government, and commercial space ventures worldwide.

Moog continues to offer a family of ESPA configurations, including Standard ESPA, ESPA Heavy, and ESPA Grande, designed to accommodate evolving payload and mission requirements. The platform’s modular architecture and adaptable interfaces support rideshare missions, payload integration, and spacecraft applications across the growing space market.

“The ESPA ring began as a technical solution to a practical challenge: maximizing every launch opportunity,” said Timothy Pargett, general manager, Moog Payload Adapters and Isolation business. “Today, it stands as a cornerstone of how missions, large and small, gain cost-effective, reliable access to orbit through rideshare. Its enduring legacy reflects visionary innovation and trusted partnerships across the aerospace community.”

In conjunction with the anniversary, a Moog flight-qualified ESPA ring will be on display at the National Museum of Nuclear Science & History in Albuquerque, N.M., from November 7, 2026, through January 10, 2027.
Museum visitors will have the opportunity to see firsthand the hardware that helped advance rideshare and enable diverse space missions.

As ESPA enters its next chapter, Moog continues to advance spacecraft payload integration and develop adaptable solutions that expand flexible, cost-effective access to orbit for future space exploration and defense missions.

Moog is a worldwide designer, manufacturer, and systems integrator of high-performance precision motion and fluid controls and control systems. Moog’s high-performance systems control military and commercial aircraft, satellites, and space vehicles, launch vehicles, defense systems, missiles, automated industrial machinery, marine, and medical equipment. Additional information about the Company can be found at www.moog.com or www.moog.com/space.

articles.title: Senate committee takes up nominees for NASA chief financial officer and inspector general
articles.author: Jeff Foust

paras.en: WASHINGTON — A Senate committee is set to advance nominations for NASA’s chief financial officer and inspector general.

The Senate Commerce Committee held a hearing Nov. 10 to consider nominations for several posts, including that of Joshua Shoemaker to be NASA’s chief financial officer and Robert Steinau to be inspector general. Those are two of the four positions at the agency that require Senate confirmation; the others are administrator and deputy administrator.

Neither nominee received many questions during the hearing, which lasted a little more than an hour. Senators largely focused their attention on the nomination of Danielle Thumann to be a member of the Federal Communications Commission.

Shoemaker is an accountant who has worked for more than 20 years in the private sector and in the Mississippi state government. Since August, he has been a senior adviser in NASA’s Mission Support Directorate, and before that was controller for the Republican National Committee.

Steinau has worked since 2009 at NASA’s Office of Inspector General, and since December 2024 has served as the office’s senior official in the absence of a Senate-confirmed inspector general. He previously worked for the Department of Energy’s Office of Inspector General and for the U.S. Secret Service.

Shoemaker, in his opening statement at the nomination hearing, said he would focus on financial accountability, improved visibility into financial performance of NASA programs, transparency with Congress on that performance and modernization of NASA financial systems.

“I believe the CFO has an important responsibility to give the administrator, NASA leadership and Congress an honest and timely picture of the agency’s financial position,” he said. He added that means how programs are performing against their planned budgets and schedules as well as ensuring effective management of resources.

He deferred questions on specific programs as well as on the proposed U.S. Space Academy that a presidential commission, led by NASA, is studying. Shoemaker said that decisions on locating the academy will ultimately be made by the president.

Steinau said that, as inspector general, he would focus on three critical challenges for NASA: returning humans to the moon, transitioning from the International Space Station to commercial stations and cybersecurity.
“NASA is moving with urgency, and it is imperative that accountability keep pace with ambition,” he said.
The Senate Commerce Committee announced Nov. 11 that it will meet Nov. 18 to vote on the nominees at the Nov. 10 hearing, sending them, if approved, to the full Senate for a confirmation vote.

NASA has been without a Senate-confirmed chief financial officer since the start of the Trump administration in January 2025. The White House nominated Greg Autry for that position in the spring of 2025, but the nomination was returned by the Senate without acting on it at the end of the year. NASA has lacked a Senate-confirmed inspector general since the departure of Paul Martin in late 2023.

articles.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5063-5069 Rocks and Chips

paras.en: Written by William Farrand, Senior Research Scientist, Space Science Institute
Earth planning date: Friday, Nov. 6, 2026

This week Curiosity has been completing its drill campaign at the “Nazca” drill hole. This is an area characterized by bedrock containing disk-shaped (or in a liberal interpretation, potato chip shaped … see linked image) crystal forms. A key objective has been to better characterize these chip-shaped features. Drill samples were delivered to the Sample Analysis for Mars (SAM) instrument. While the SAM analysis was on-going, Monday’s plan included a ChemCam LIBS observation of another crystal-form, “Ahi Veremos,” more Mastcam frames to fill out a mosaic of the Nazca near to mid-field, and environmental observations including a large dust devil survey, and horizon and atmospheric zenith movies.

A long distance Remote Micro-Imager (RMI) mosaic of rock clusters below the “Cordillera” ridge was also collected. Mastcam collected more frames of its Nazca mosaic, and more environmental observations were made.

Friday’s planning was for three sols with three targeted science blocks and a drive away from the Nazca drill site. A MAHLI mosaic of the side of the block that hosts the Nazca drill hole was planned. It was also planned to use MAHLI’s nighttime white-light and ultraviolet LED lamps for nighttime imaging of the crystal-forms. Mars’ moon, Phobos, was eclipsing the Sun and imaging of that event was prioritized. ChemCam LIBS observations were planned for each sol including a cluster of crystal forms, a resistant layer in the side of the Nazca block and a dark float rock. A long distance RMI mosaic of dark lenses beneath a planar surface on the “Mishe Mokwa” ridge was to be made. Another round of environmental observation was also planned. Finally, Friday’s drive was to take the rover back towards its southerly trending route where Curiosity would continue its trek of exploration and discovery.

articles.title: Scotland’s Flow Country

paras.en: Compared to ecosystems in many other parts of the world, the blanket bogs of the Flow Country in northern Scotland are unassuming—soggy, treeless landscapes dominated by hummocky mosses, grasses, and heathers. Yet, to ecologists, the seemingly desolate areas are nothing short of extraordinary.

The bogs store tremendous quantities of carbon. That’s because their soils are so waterlogged that microbes cannot fully break down dead plant material, a process that would otherwise release carbon dioxide. Instead, partially decayed plant matter accumulates into thick layers of spongy, crumbly, carbon-rich material called peat.

The unusual ecosystems, also called blanket mires and featherbed bogs, only occur in places with abundant rainfall, poor drainage, and low levels of evapotranspiration. These types of bogs cover just 120,000 square kilometers (46,000 square miles) globally, less than one-tenth of one percent of Earth’s land surface. The image above, captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8, is centered on blanket bogs in the Scottish Highlands, home to the largest such ecosystem in Europe. This peatland is also the first of its type to be inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The peat bogs of northern Scotland, home to more than 30 species of sphagnum moss, are spread across some 1,900 square kilometers (730 square miles) of the country’s Highlands region. In this image, boggy areas appear dark brown and are sprinkled with lakes. The light green area on the right side around Thurso is farmland. The darker green geometric patterns in the center are conifer plantations. The image was captured in the spring, the part of the year when the land surface is most waterlogged and peat bogs begin to accumulate large amounts of new biomass.

paras.en: While forests store most of their carbon in living trees—which eventually release it back into the atmosphere when they burn or die—peat bogs often store carbon for many thousands of years. Some parts of the Flow Country have been accumulating peat for more than 9,000 years, building deposits exceeding eight meters thick, according to UNESCO. Overall, scientists estimate that all of the world’s peatlands cover just 3 percent of Earth’s land surface but store more than 600 gigatons of carbon—about twice as much as all the world’s forests combined.

articles.title: Sudan war: First ‘suicide’ drone attacks, now long-range strikes are the norm

paras.en: Sudan war: First ‘suicide’ drone attacks, now long-range strikes are the norm

Drones and drought are “closing in” on Sudan, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), said on Tuesday, describing unprecedented attacks on the country’s infrastructure including by drones travelling up to 1,500 kilometres before hitting their target.

“It is an assault unlike anything Sudan has seen before. In the last week of October, not a single day passed without a drone strike on a power station in Sudan. Up to 15 were hit in the month of October,” said agency spokesperson James Elder.

“This year in Sudan, two in three child casualties were killed by armed drones. They are bringing war to places that were once safe. People in Sudan talk about three things: they talk about safety, education and water. Drones are taking all three.”
The UNICEF alert comes amid ongoing fighting between former allies turned military rivals the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

Well over 15 million people urgently require shelter across the country but drone strikes on civilians, markets and key public infrastructure continue to hinder aid efforts and increase the suffering of non-combatants.
“Several years ago, there was a use of suicide drones, which was terrifying to see that in Sudan,” Mr. Elder explained.

Highlighting the use of increasingly accurate long-range drones in the last 12 months, including some travelling 1,500 kilometres, he explained that it was impossible for humanitarian agencies like UNICEF to ascertain who was behind “at least 15 strikes” on Sudanese power stations in October. “One would struggle to think if it was in the interest of the SAF, of Government, to do that,” he added.

Straight off the plane from Sudan, Mr. Elder told journalists in Geneva about one of the many young war victims he had met from El Obeid, where UN Human Rights Council investigators say that civilians live in constant fear of drone attack.

“Buri is a teenager. An explosive took both his hands. He lives in a tent. He told me, ‘I must accept this,’” Mr. Elder explained. “He spends the mornings learning online and the afternoons picking grass for animals with stumps for hands. His friends help him, that’s Sudan. It’s relentless. It’s crushing.”

Like Ukraine, Sudan’s energy sector is being struck repeatedly, but unlike in Ukraine, Sudanese targets are not repaired, the UNICEF spokesperson stressed: “When a power station is struck, water pumps stop, water treatment stops. Families are forced into expensive and unsafe alternatives.”
Harvests suffer, prices keep rising and food slips further and further out of reach
In addition, disease is spreading, the agency warns, with pockets of cholera identified and the cold chain for vaccines and medicines increasingly threatened by the ongoing war.
Farmers are also losing the ability to irrigate crops because their pumps run on electricity generators which are too expensive to operate because of “crippling” fuel shortages, Mr. Elder continued.

“Harvests suffer, prices keep rising and food slips further and further out of reach: a lethal cycle kicks in…All this at a time when an estimated 825,000 children under five in Sudan are expected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year; the type that kills.”
As part of the wider UN response, UNICEF and partners have treated hundreds of thousands of children for the deadliest form of malnutrition.

The agency has provided healthcare to more than 2.5 million people and vaccinated millions of children against deadly diseases. Teams have also repaired and hooked up water systems to solar power, helping to keep safe water flowing for close to eight million people.

But with “so many crises happening at once, everything, everything is at breaking point”, Mr. Elder said, noting that UNICEF’s response in Sudan is just one-third funded. “Resilience cannot run on goodwill alone,” he insisted.

articles.title: From Japan to Rwanda, early warnings are saving lives – but millions remain unprotected

paras.en: From Japan to Rwanda, early warnings are saving lives – but millions remain unprotected

Early warning systems are saving lives across the globe, but for millions of people the warning never arrives, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on Wednesday, urging the world to protect every person on Earth by the end of 2027.

“No one should lose their life simply because a warning came too late – or never came at all,” he told a high-level event on the Early Warnings for All initiative at the COP31 climate conference, which runs until 20 November in Antalya, Türkiye.

His appeal came as a new report from the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) showed that 136 countries – 70 per cent of the total – now report having multi-hazard early warning systems, 17 more than in March 2025.
Yet major gaps remain in the most vulnerable countries, as a powerful El Niño raises the stakes.

The report, Global Status of Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems 2026, finds that countries with substantial to comprehensive systems record disaster-related mortality 6.1 times lower than those with limited to moderate ones, and 3.2 times fewer people affected.

It also shows what that means on the ground. When a magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck off Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula in July 2025, the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center issued its first threat messages within 10 minutes.

Japan evacuated approximately 1.9 million people, while in Ecuador’s Galápagos islands, more than 2,300 people were moved out of high-risk areas hours before waves of about 1.3 metres reached the shore.

In Madagascar, an early action plan developed by the Malagasy Red Cross was partially activated before Tropical Cyclone Gezani made landfall in February, with some 600 door-to-door visits reaching 80,000 to 100,000 people with warnings and evacuation support.

And in Rwanda’s Karongi district, a tea farmer and her daughters were warned – through women’s cooperatives, SMS, local radio and loudspeakers – that heavy rain was expected within 48 hours, giving her time to reinforce her terraces, clear water channels and store her dried tea leaves before the downpour.

Around one in three countries still has no early warning system, Mr. Guterres said, with the widest gaps in least developed countries, small island developing States and countries affected by conflict.
“They did the least to cause the climate crisis, but are being hit first and hardest,” he said.
“Some European countries have more weather stations that meet global standards than the entire continent of Africa,” the Secretary-General added. “We cannot warn people about what we cannot see.”
WMO chief Celeste Saulo warned that the current El Niño “could be literally off our monitoring charts”.
“While we cannot stop El Niño, we can prevent many of its worst human consequences,” she said.
Urging countries to “accelerate and build systems that last”, Mr. Guterres set out three priorities:
- making early warnings a permanent public service;
- closing financing and capacity gaps; and
- moving from fragmented projects to coordinated, long-term support for country-led plans.

Since 2022, some $2 billion has been mobilised and around 160 countries are receiving support, he noted. But finance must cover the entire warning chain, he said; “from weather forecasting to communication tools to volunteers knocking on doors”.
Warnings are also increasingly triggering action before disaster strikes: in 2025, 146 anticipatory action activations in 54 countries reached 9.6 million people, the report found.
“Countries have made significant progress in strengthening their early warning systems, but too many people remain unprotected,” said Kamal Kishore, head of UNDRR.
“The climate crisis is accelerating. Our protection of people must accelerate with it,” Mr. Guterres said. “Together, let us make sure that every warning arrives in time.”

articles.title: Gaza winter aid: ‘No more delay’, Fletcher tells governments stalling on support

paras.en: Gaza winter aid: ‘No more delay’, Fletcher tells governments stalling on support

The UN’s Emergency Relief Coordinator, Tom Fletcher, expressed deep concern about the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza, as UN member states and partners have been repeatedly delaying sending their support to the Strip.

“Foreign Ministers and partners have assured me of support, but also repeatedly said that progress would be hard until after Israeli elections. Now we’re told to wait for the formation of a Government,” he said.
“In case anyone has any doubt about international humanitarian law: this is not an acceptable excuse, as the international community and Board of Peace have made clear,” Mr. Fletcher stressed.
With winter underway, people living in Gaza are facing ever-harsher living conditions, including freezing temperatures and harsh storms which collapse or flood the tents thousands are living in.

“What makes this even more infuriating is that they are at this needless risk from weather that is not a threat where decent shelter exists. And would not be such a threat had we been able to supply decent tents and essential Winter kit,” Mr. Fletcher said.
The UN relief chief stressed that the UN had a “clear plan” for which supplies need to reach Gaza, “not in weeks, but weeks ago,” with each delay costing lives.

The list includes durable shelter, warm clothes, blankets, bedding and safe heating solutions, as well as generators, fuel, engine oil, spare parts, equipment to pump out water, remove debris and clear explosive ordnance.

“No more delay. Open all the crossings, not just one. Let our vital NGO partners work. Allow the commercial markets to function. Stop this collective punishment. Fund the plan. End this predictable, preventable suffering,” he urged.

The UN’s labour agency (ILO) on Wednesday, called on international partners to increase their financial support for a jobs-led recovery plan in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT), which aims to lay the conditions for long-term resilience and stability.

“Humanitarian assistance alone cannot restore livelihoods, essential services, or the institutional foundations needed for sustainable recovery,” said Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov.

In Gaza alone, 252,000 jobs were lost between the third quarters of 2023 and 2025, unemployment reached a staggering 85.1 per cent and labour income losses totalled $2.77 billion, with women and young people facing particularly limited prospects.
“Behind every job lost is a person, a family and a future placed at risk,” said ILO Director-General Gilbert F. Houngbo.
The ILO’s Decent Work and Recovery Programme (DWRP) supports emergency employment, enterprise recovery, social protection and stronger labour institutions to address the issue.
Over the past three years, it has helped generate approximately 130,000 paid workdays and contributed to social allowances reaching over 30,000 older persons and persons with disabilities.

articles.title: Age-old rivalry bookends RLWC but will it end 18 years of supremacy?

paras.en: Australia vs New Zealand: Age-old rivalry bookends Rugby League World Cup but will it end 18 years of supremacy?

In the men's and women's Rugby League World Cup finals Australia will take on New Zealand; the last time both New Zealand teams won the tournament was back in 2008, nearly two decades ago; the finals take place on Sunday November 16

An age-old rivalry will bookend the Rugby League World Cup 2026 in the latest symbol that rugby league worldwide has grown but, ultimately, the contenders are still just contenders and the favourites remain just that.
In a sensational opener to the tournament, Australia clinched a dramatic 24-22 victory over New Zealand in front of the biggest Test crowd in 50 years, surpassing the previous benchmark set in 1974.
Now, the two men's teams will meet once again to decide who will be world champions. And in the women's tournament, the same showdown will decide who is on top.

- Download Sky Sports app for analysis, news and video

Australia and New Zealand have contested the last four women's World Cup finals. In the men's, Australia have cemented their spot as ever with New Zealand returning to the final for the first time since 2013.

New Zealand's men's side have won the World Cup just once back in 2008. The women's side have won it on three occasions but not in 18 years, their last glory coming back in 2008 - the last year New Zealand were on top of the world.
Since then, it has been total and utter Australian domination. New Zealand Women head into their fifth final in a row against the Jillaroos. They do not want it to be a fifth loss in a row.

Coming into this Rugby League World Cup, the talk was all about the new contenders, the ones that had been growing and growing and looked like, this time, they could take down the big boys. The talk was all about Tonga and Samoa showing the landscape of rugby league internationally had changed.
Throughout the group stage, they looked primed and their showdown in the final pool round, in which Tonga came away 20-18 victors, seemed to be the marker that they were here for the big win.
In the end, that match between the two nations ultimately became their final of sorts.
Following that, Tonga succumbed to New Zealand and Samoa fell short of Australia in the men's semi-finals. Exciting Samoa Women could not keep up in a 32-0 loss to New Zealand Women.
They edged closer in some respects but could not complete the job.
The task is set for New Zealand's men - do what they did 18 years ago and release Australia's near two-decade long grip on the title.

Kalyn Ponga became the emblem of how the change to State of Origin eligibility would open up the international landscape as he could still play for Queensland but also represent his heritage. He did that valiantly by returning from a broken arm in that opening clash within just 22 days to star in the semi-finals.
What it would mean to him to complete the journey.
The World Cup storyline, for many, was going to be how a nation could defy the odds to win and send shockwaves globally.
While on the face of it New Zealand winning seems normal, it is anything but. They can still change the landscape, mark their moment, move the competition on.
A victory for them means Australia will be denied the chance to say they have been world champions for 20 years - surely that is as good a motivation as any?
One bookend is a win for Australia. Could the other bookend be glory for New Zealand?

articles.title: Cummins to address Khawaja 'Sandpapergate' claims on Friday

paras.en: 'Sandpapergate': Australia captain Pat Cummins to address Usman Khawaja claims on Friday

Usman Khawaja says in new book 'Sabr' that every Australia player was aware of ball-tampering scheme in Cape Town in 2018; current Test captain Pat Cummins confirms he's "happy to speak with any and all media" on Friday; white-ball skipper for England series Mitch Marsh declined to comment

Australia captain Pat Cummins has called a press conference for Friday to have his say on 'Sandpapergate' after former team-mate Usman Khawaja's explosive claims that the entire dressing room knew about the ball-tampering scheme that took place on the tour of South Africa in 2018.
Khawaja made the revelations in his new book 'Sabr', bringing the scandal back onto the agenda after eight years.
Cummins has been rested for the white-ball series' against England, which also begins on Friday with the first ODI in Perth, but has publicly invited a media grilling in Sydney for that same morning.

"I'm training at Cricket Central (in Sydney) tomorrow morning before the Blues play in the Shield match," Cummins posted on X on Thursday. "Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week at 9.30 am.
"I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly."

In the immediate aftermath of the Cape Town Test in 2018, in which Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball, only he, then captain Steve Smith and David Warner - who said on Monday that Khawaja's version of events was "100 per cent accurate" - were banned.

Khawaja's revelations have invited renewed speculation over the role of the bowling group who benefitted from the ball manipulation - with Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon having previously distanced themselves from the episode.

In 2021, the quartet issued a carefully worded statement responding to "rumour mongering and innuendo" in which they denied knowing that a foreign substance had been taken onto the field to alter the ball in order to try and make it swing.
Cricket Australia chairman David Boon has backed Cummins, saying his job as skipper is not under threat.

"We absolutely support Pat," Boon said in comments published by The Australian on Thursday. "He's been an exemplary captain, he's led the team with integrity and, you know, very successfully over the period of time that he's been captain, so there's no question of our confidence in him continuing on in that fact."

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, after Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg insisted there would be no re-opening of the 'Sandpapergate' investigation, Starc said of Khawaja's claims: "I haven't really paid much attention to it to be fair.
"There are differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process, at the time and since.
"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but from where I stand my opinion hasn't changed, my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.
"As far as our statement said, we weren't aware of things being taken on the field. That's where I'll leave it.
"I will be sticking to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time eight years ago, so clearly there are differing versions from different people.
"We weren't aware of anything taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen in Cape Town.
"As far as the book is concerned, I haven't read it. I probably won't read it, so that's for Usman to elaborate on."
On Khawaja saying the ball was also tampered with in the Test before the Cape Town fixture, at Port Elizabeth, now Gqeberha, Starc added: "That's the first I was aware of any of that."
Starc, Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon are not part of the upcoming white-ball series at home to England.
Marsh not drawn on Khawaja claims | Root: It's all speculation

Captain of Australia for the three-match ODI series and five T20s against England, Mitchell Marsh - who was in the Test team that toured South Africa in 2018 - declined to comment at a press conference in Perth on Thursday.
"I respect (Khawaja) for telling his story and for writing his book, and I don't sit here coming from a place of judgment on any of that," Marsh said ahead of Friday's series-opening ODI.
"It was a really tough time for Australian cricket. There's still a lot of people hurting. Now is not the time for me to share my story.
"My honest answer is because I've personally moved on. I respect that others probably haven't, but I have. And I hope that's respected."

He added: "Everyone's got their story. Some will be willing to share it, and others might not, purely on the basis of the fact that they've moved on. I think it's really important that at some stage we do."
In his book, Khawaja also said Australia experimented with lifting the seam on the ball during the 2017-18 Ashes at home to England, which they won 4-0 under the captaincy of Smith.
The ECB said 'no comment' when approached by Sky Sports News.
"It's all speculation. I wasn't in that dressing room. I don't know what went on. I don't want to speculate, as I said. My focus is with this (ODI) team right now and what we've got coming up."
Cricket Australia: No compelling reason to re-open 'Sandpapergate' case

A statement from the Australian Cricketers' Association called the 2018 scandal a "low point for Australian cricket" for which Smith, Warner and Bancroft paid an "enormous" and "disproportionate" price.

The statement added: "There are no winners in this issue, and nothing can undo what happened. There are humans in the centre of this and we will be calling for the ongoing vitriol directed at those involved to come to an end."

Greenberg, who was not part of Cricket Australia at the time of the scandal, told Australian radio station SEN on the decision not to launch a fresh inquiry: "We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this again.
"I don't think there's anything that can be gained from that.
"We have said we're comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we've received. That includes what we've seen from Usman. Our position hasn't changed on that.

"There's absolutely no benefit in going back, that's the clear position of the CA board. I think it's fine, we've got to look ahead, and the matter was dealt with under a previous leadership back in 2018.
"Trying to second-guess decisions from a previous time or making an assessment through the prism of hindsight is not something we want to do."
'Usman's version of events inconsistent with what others say'
The Cricket Australia CEO added: "When you cut to the core of the challenge that we face here, Usman's version of events is inconsistent with what others have had to say.
"I can assure you there are lots of other players who have a very, very different version of events and they have made that very public from the very start of 2018.
"They have been very consistent in their position right through until today. From my conversations with many over the weekend, I don't think that will change either.
"I think we end up at the same intersection point, which is that eight years ago people have a version of events which differ from each other.
"No one would like to get this chapter of Australian cricket closed more than me, but it is unlikely."

Former Australia captain Michael Clarke hopes the truth comes to light, saying that chance was missed in the wake of the scandal in 2018 and then again three years later when Bancroft replied it was "probably self-explanatory" after being asked whether the bowling attack knew of the sandpaper use.

Clarke told 2DayFM: "[Australia fans] can't trust what's real. They don't know the truth until this gets reopened and the truth comes out. I would just like to see whatever the truth is for it all to come out, allow people to move on.

"For me, right now, there are more questions than answers. I want to know, firstly, did everyone know? Because certain players have come out and said they didn't. That's important information so we can get the truth.
"I can't believe we haven't heard from Cummins yet. Steve Smith lost his job. If this doesn't happen, Tim Paine never captains Australia. And neither does Cummins.
"Cummins would not have captained a game at this stage if 'Sandpapergate' didn't happen because Smith would still be captain."

articles.title: Darts star Sheldon on brilliant Beau and the Littler effect hitting Ireland

paras.en: Darts player Katie Sheldon: Irish ace on brilliant Beau Greaves and how Littler Littler has inspired a boom in Ireland

Katie Sheldon talks about Beau Greaves and how Littler Littler is inspiring the next generation of players in Ireland; 'Beau 'n' Arrow' faces Littler at the Grand Slam of Darts; you can watch the tournament in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports from November 14-22
Katie Sheldon - nicknamed 'The Dublin Diamond' - is a pioneer of women's darts in Ireland at the tender age of 22.
As one of the hottest prospects to come out of the Emerald Isle, Sheldon has already competed on the Women's Series and at the Women's World Matchplay held at the iconic Winter Gardens in Blackpool.
Currently working as a wire assembler, Sheldon has already become the World Masters girls' champion and a two-time WDF World Cup team winner.
- Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results 📅
- Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
- Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺

"I keep saying that one goal of mine is to pick up a PDC title, so a Women's Series. And along with that, it's trying to qualify for the Women's World Matchplay," she told Sky Sports, having taken part in the Netflix 'Beat Luke Littler' challenge in which she was given the chance to win £501,000.

It wasn't to be for Sheldon over one leg against 'The Nuke', but she has bigger dreams of emulating brilliant Beau Greaves, who finished a dominant season on the PDC Women's Series by winning 17 out of 24 events.

The Doncaster thrower will be at the Grand Slam of Darts where she has been drawn with Luke Littler and Niels Zonneveld. She also secured her qualification for the world championship at Alexandra Palace alongside 'Beat Luke Littler' winner Fallon Sherrock, Gemma Hayter, 'The Lancashire Rose' Lisa Ashton, and Belgian-born Swedish darts player, Vicky Pruim.

'Beau 'n' Arrow' made history in April by becoming the first woman to win a PDC ranking title at Players Championship 11 in Milton Keynes, defeating three former world champions, Rob Cross, Gary Anderson and Michael Smith.

She has risen to 75th in the PDC Order of Merit with the youngster closing in on the world's top 64, an achievement that would have ramifications for her future in the Women's Series with female players who break into the top 64 globally and hold a Tour Card restricted from playing in the Women's Series.
"She's really a great talent, and she's pushed us all," said Sheldon. "I think her being there has actually brought the standard up.
"Her being there has been a massive help to all of the women to progress their game, but I think it would be a sad loss to the Women's Series when she's gone."
The success of two-time back-to-back world champion Littler has played a huge part in the surge of youth academies - not least in Ireland where Sheldon has seen a surge in interest.
She explained: "I think Luke has given everyone that [interest]. I think a lot of people have started picking up darts, but mainly youths.
"When I played youth darts in youth academies, there wasn't that many of us, a couple of lads, but the numbers are just through the roof now.
"We have a Dublin academy, and I think at the team event, there was 183 kids there at the weekend, just playing darts for their local teams and clubs, which is amazing for the sport.
"It's great to see the growth, and I think a lot of that is down to what Luke's done."
'People probably don't know what they're witnessing'
Despite his success, Littler has threatened to boycott certain tournaments after being booed and whistled by vociferous crowds - not least in the Netherlands and Germany.
Sheldon accepts "it's a hard one to take" for players as well as Littler, himself.
She said: "When he first came on the scene, everyone was bigging him up and it was great, but then you're turning up to tournaments and people are booing him.
"People probably don't know what they're witnessing at the minute. The standard of darts is just crazy.

"I think if you are a fan, you should be going there to enjoy it. Don't get me wrong, everyone loves singing the songs, but I think there should be just that level of respect for the players when they're playing because at the end of the day, this is their livelihood as well.
"They want to be trying to perform the best for the fans, and they probably can't do that with all the boos.
"It's one of those things he has to deal with, which is kind of sad to see."

articles.title: Ex-wife of police prosecutor tells court of 'frightening' abuse
articles.author: Tony Ibrahim

paras.en: A police prosecutor convicted of domestic violence offences was read victim impact statements from his ex-wife and her children.
His ex-wife said the assaults she endured "changed the course of my life and the life of my children".
The matter was adjourned for sentencing at Gosford District Court on December 11.
A NSW police prosecutor assaulted his then wife as she held their newborn baby while recovering from birth complications, a court has heard.
MZ, whose identity the court suppressed to protect the victim, was taken into custody in July, after a jury convicted him of 11 offences related to domestic violence.

These include two counts of sexual intercourse without consent, two counts of common assault, five counts of assault occasioning bodily harm, intentionally choke a person without consent, and sexually touch another person without consent.
The 50-year-old man, a police prosecutor whose career with the force spanned more than two decades, appeared via audio-visual link in the NSW District Court.
He sat idle and expressionless as his ex-wife and her two children read victim impact statements.
"You did not simply hurt me, you changed the course of my life and the life of my children," his ex-wife read from the courtroom.
She read through pages of testimony maintaining composure, but her voice began to waver when she detailed the abuse her children had to witness.
"After the C-section of our second child, you assaulted me when I was recovering from complications," she said.
"I was physically weak and recovering…My eldest daughter had to intervene to protect me from you."
One incident, she said, caused her to realise he would not change.
"The time when you assaulted me when I held our child was one of the most frightening moments.
"Even holding our baby was not enough to stop you. That's when I began to understand that nothing would make you stop."
The court heard that she faced a power imbalance when accusing a police prosecutor of domestic violence offences.
"The blue shirt you hid behind was meant to represent safety…instead it became the same blue shirt I learnt to fear," she said.
She also said the years spent pursuing the matter through the courts forced her to relive trauma.
"You do not get to write the end of my story," she said. "I survived everything you did. I survived you."
The court heard the abuse left her two children suffering from post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and living with a distrust of law enforcement.
Court heard MZ was sexually abused as a child
Judge Philip Hogan heard closing arguments as members of MZ's family watched from the gallery, among them his father, brothers and sister.
The defence, represented by barrister Arjun Chhabra, said the serious offences warranted a jail sentence of just under 10 years after mitigating factors were considered.
"MZ described an incident of sexual abuse when he was a child by a trusted figure," the court heard.

Mr Chhabra said his client had been diagnosed with PTSD, and that his work as a police prosecutor exposed him to criminal matters that left him triggered — particularly around an incident of domestic violence in 2020.
"It is likely that his symptoms reduced his capacity to manage stress during periods of heightened conflict," Mr Chhabra said.
He said MZ's career in the NSW Police Force would make him a target in jail, and that the time he would serve in protective custody would be more onerous.
"That he may come face to face with people he arrested or prosecuted…that is a real punishment… and that ought to be reflected in the sentencing exercise," Mr Chhabra said.
The Crown, represented by barrister Rohan Cooley, said a serving police officer should have known better.
"The offender must have known because he was a police officer that this would be a consequence," he said.
He acknowledged the report of sexual abuse and PTSD, but did not believe it "impaired his ability to appreciate the seriousness or potential consequences of his actions".
Mr Cooley told the court MZ had shown no sense of wrongdoing over his actions.
"There's clearly no expression of remorse," he said.
The defence had previously acknowledged the absence of an expression of remorse.
Judge Hogan adjourned the matter for sentencing at Gosford District Court on December 11.
He has been suspended from the NSW Police Force without pay while his employment is under review.

articles.title: Data centre industry butts up against community challenges
articles.author: Evelyn Leckie and Thomas Kelsall

paras.en: The industry body for data centre proponents says its members are battling community hesitancy and policy uncertainty.
It comes amid calls by minor parties for SA to halt approvals for new centres.
The state government is preparing legislation to regulate the industry.

The peak body representing data centres in Australia say its members are still grappling with "getting community consultation right" after several AI companies have either dumped or paused their plans for building centres across the country.

South Australia has today seen the first sign of data centre development in retreat, with Quantum DC announcing it will pause plans to build a 1200-megawatt AI data centre in Tungkillo, in the Adelaide Hills, following deep frustration, anger and protests from the surrounding community.

In New South Wales, another AI data centre proposed for Sydney's south, on the Cooks River, was scrapped over the weekend, the latest in a series of proposed NSW data centres to be dumped following community opposition.
Peak body Data Centres Australia does not represent Quantum DC.
Speaking broadly, its CEO Belinda Dennett said the challenge with community engagement was choosing the right time.
"Communities want early engagement, but they also want detailed answers, so there is a bit of a trade-off.
"Often, early engagement means you don't have all those answers around design plans, around energy source, around how much water that may use."
She said there was great potential and interest to build data centres in South Australia, but operators and investors wanted policy certainty.
"That's the challenge for all the states at the moment, the challenge of not having federal rules in place … we don't have that policy certainty," she said.
"The quicker we have certainty, the more viable I think Australia's going to be."

On Thursday, political parties including the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens welcomed the pause on the Tungkillo development, while the SA government criticised the developer for its consultation process.
The Greens went a step further, calling for a data centre moratorium.

SA's minister for artificial intelligence (AI), Chris Picton, said the Tungkillo announcement highlighted why the state government was keen to get legislation through the parliament to enable proper regulatory control.

"[It's] going to be critical to making sure that we can think through all these issues with data centres to make sure that can be managed in an appropriate way, whether that be issues about energy, or water, or land use," Mr Picton said.

Opposition leader Ashton Hurn said it didn't make sense for a data centre at Tungkillo to be built on "prime agricultural land", but there was also a need to make sure the community understood why data centres are needed.
"No-one really wants them in the backyard because no-one really understands what they're needed for in the first place,"
"We believe that a vehicle to do that is including them in the royal commission," Ms Hurn said.
When details of the state's Royal Commission into Artificial Intelligence were released in early October, its terms of reference did not include data centres.
Mr Picton said it wasn't remiss of the government not to include them: "They are completely separate things.
"Data centres have issues, but they're infrastructure issues … They're issues about energy use, water use and where the land is."
The Greens, One Nation and the Liberal Party united in the upper house on Wednesday to establish a parliamentary inquiry into data centres, which was not supported by Labor.
One Nation SA leader Cory Bernardi said the party would like to see a pause on data centres until the inquiry is finished.
"But we're also recognising that data centres per se are not bad," he said.
"We have a data centre here in the metropolitan area of Adelaide that hasn't caused any fuss at all.
"But what we want is a community licence for it."

articles.title: Kiwi duo Ponga and Waaka claim Golden Boot wins after stunning seasons

paras.en: New Zealand duo Kalyn Ponga and Stacey Waaka have been named the men's and women's Golden Boot winners after outstanding individual seasons.
Ponga scored six tries as he led Newcastle to the NRL grand final before scoring two further tries for the Kiwis at the Rugby League World Cup despite a broken arm.
Waaka, a cross-code star, scored nine tries for the Warriors in just 10 NRLW appearances and added nine tries in four World Cup appearances.
Both players will be in action for New Zealand's men's and women's sides in their respective World Cup finals this weekend as they take on Australia.
Ponga is New Zealand's eighth men's Golden Boot winner, joining Hugh McGahan, Stacey Jones, Benji Marshall, Shaun Johnson, Roger Tuivasa-Sheck, Joseph Manu, James Fisher-Harris.
Waaka is the third New Zealand player to win the women's award, joining Raecene McGregor and Georgia Hale.

articles.title: Mississippi's Scott Colom secures Senate seat in another midterm win for Democrats

paras.en: Mississippi's Scott Colom secures Senate seat in another midterm win for Democrats
Colom beats Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, will be 1st Black senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction era

Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, and will become the state's first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it will echo through the country as well.

The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South.

The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favour after local election officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist.
Election workers tally absentee ballots in Jackson, Miss., on Wednesday. (Ellen Schmidt/The Associated Press)
Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state's large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith's missteps as she sought a second full term.
Colom waged an aggressive campaign to take advantage of a tough national environment for Republicans and the fact that Mississippi has a larger share of Black voters than any other state.
"They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," he said in the campaign's closing stretch.
He also said he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.

"It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better, and we don't come up with excuses as to why we can't do it."
Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer celebrated the win on social media.

"Scott Colom is the only person who could've gotten this done," Schumer wrote. "Along with his staff and volunteers, Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what's possible for Democrats in the South."

Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate. Former president Bill Clinton and former vice-president Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom's behalf in the campaign's closing weeks.

Despite this support, the contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention from Democrats who belatedly infused cash into Colom's candidacy well after Black senators, including Georgia's Raphael Warnock and Maryland's Angela Alsobrooks, urged donors and party leaders to see the contest as winnable.

The son of a one-time Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallized.
Colom attracted particular notice for some of the year's most widely circulated ads.

After Hyde-Smith, 67, seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they'd "pick another senator instead."

When Trump came to Corinth, Miss., in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.
Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: "Is this not the best president in our lifetime?"
U.S. President Donald Trump and Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith are seen at a rally in Corinth, Miss., on Oct. 26. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)
"I love that," Trump replied when he continued his 80-plus minutes at the microphone. "Sometimes they get up and they talk for 10 minutes."

The appearance tracked Colom's tactic of criticizing Trump's policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him.

Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a non-entity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.
There is some irony to Hyde-Smith finding herself flat-footed against Colom.

In 2022, then president Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. The state's senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chair, backed the nomination.
Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom's confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president's choices for federal judicial positions in their home state.
- Republicans took big hits in the U.S. midterms. Does that mean Trump's political era is over?
- Senior Democratic congressman says party 'going to put an end' to Trump's tariffs
Colom said his Senate bid was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.

The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family.

"In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection," Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy during the Second World War, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction.
"He was killed for helping Mississippians vote," Colom said. "On Tuesday, use your vote and honour everyone who died for that right."

With the largest share of Black voters of any state, Mississippi's general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbours. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just three percentage points.

Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats' usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.

Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.

Then-Gov. Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who'd also been Mississippi's first Black congressman since Reconstruction.

During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story.

"My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision and the values," he said, "and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I've done that they shouldn't get a chance."

articles.title: 2 dead, 4 critically injured after building collapses in New York City

paras.en: 2 dead, 4 critically injured after building collapses in New York City
Firefighters dig through rubble of 3-storey building that fell at edge of construction site

Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-storey building in New York City's Brooklyn borough on Wednesday after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least two people and trapping others beneath the wreckage.

Firefighters were called to the scene in the Flatbush neighbourhood at about 4 p.m. News helicopter footage showed dozens of firefighters scouring the debris, with a group homing in on one area and appearing to use a saw to cut through the wreckage.
At least 17 people were hospitalized with injuries, including four in critical condition, officials said during a news conference.

New York City Fire Department (FDNY) officials said their search-and-rescue operations would continue into the night. "We do not know how many people were missing overall," said the FDNY's chief of department, John Esposito. It was unclear whether people might still be trapped.

"This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation, with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "This type of rescue is exactly what the FDNY trains for."
Firefighters search through the rubble on Wednesday. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
About 250 firefighters were working at the scene, Mamdani said.

At about 6:30 p.m., firefighters pulled a dust-covered person — still alive and moving — out of a hole they had dug into the rubble pile, hoisting them up on a stretcher and rushing them to a waiting ambulance.

The building that collapsed — a mixed-use structure with apartments sitting atop businesses — had been perched at the edge of a lot where another one-storey building had been torn down for a construction project. The site was being excavated, and the building that fell down filled the construction pit with bricks and wood.
New York City's buildings commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, said that at the time of the disaster, construction workers were on site doing excavation work adjacent to the building that collapsed.
A wall was shorn off an adjacent Brooklyn building, exposing a bedroom and closets filled with clothing inside. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.

A drone hovered over the site as firefighters dug by hand, tossing chunks of rubble aside. Rescuers also used dogs to sniff for survivors. As darkness fell, firefighters used flashlights to illuminate the area where they worked.
New York's fire commissioner, Lillian Bonsignore, said the rescue teams were performing "dangerous and perilous" work. "Every move is choreographed," she said.
One firefighter sustained minor injuries, fire officials said.
First responders rescue a person from the rubble of the collapse. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
Phone and email messages seeking comment were left with the architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project.
One resident of the collapsed building, Anderson Velez, told the New York Post he was at work when his wife called and said she and their two children, aged 7 and 2, were trapped in the wreckage.
"She called me when the building collapsed while she was inside with rubble on top of her. She was screaming for someone to help get my son out and then the call cut off," he said.
Velez said he later learned that his family had been pulled from the rubble alive.

articles.title: Hegseth, wife and aides spark scolding from guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

paras.en: Hegseth, wife and aides spark scolding from guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
Pentagon spokesperson said U.S. army sentinel 'correctly and respectfully' called for proper decorum

A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony.
Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that "all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesperson, said that "while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured — and will always honour — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe," he added.
Incident follows near impeachment of Hegseth

The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from the First and Second World Wars and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," since 1948.
Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that was also attended by U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance.
The incident comes a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress.

The effort was led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach him. With Democrats set to take control of the House of Representatives and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.
Hegseth slammed the effort on Tuesday at his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the U.S. Constitution for his removal.

A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.
"On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime," Hegseth said Tuesday.
"This is not patriotism," he said. "This is sabotage."
Following the reprimand at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, the reaction from Democrats was swift.
Rep. Gwen Moore said Hegseth demonstrated "his utter lack of fitness for his office."

"One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier," she wrote in a social media post.
It was not the first time members of Trump's team have caused controversy at Arlington National Cemetery.

During his campaign for a second term, Trump attended a ceremony in 2024 to honour U.S. forces killed in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. A campaign staffer reportedly shoved a cemetery employee trying to prevent two people from filming and photographing the event.

Trump, who had been invited by troops' families, later shared a video on TikTok showing him at the cemetery with a voiceover blaming the Biden administration for the "disaster" of the Afghanistan withdrawal.
U.S. law prohibits campaign or election-related activities within national military cemeteries.

articles.title: Iran classes Argentina navy, air force as 'terrorist organizations'

paras.en: Iran's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday that it classified Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations."

In early April, Argentina designated Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a "terrorist organization," as US President Donald Trump pressured his allies to do so following the war on Iran.
Tehran's designation came "based on the principle of reciprocity," Iran's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
"It is evident that the responsibility for all consequences arising from this matter will lie with the Argentine government," the ministry added, without a mention of Argentina's army.
Iran passed a legislation in 2019 that grants retaliatory measures against states that designate its military as a terrorist group.
Argentina holds Hezbollah responsible for deadly attacks
Argentina said in April that it had taken action against the IRGC because of its support for the Lebanon-based militant group Hezbollah.
Buenos Aires holds Hezbollah responsible for the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center, which killed 85 people.
IRGC classified as a terrorist group by many countries
IRGC was established at the end of Iran's 1979 Islamic Revolution as an elite armed militia whose role was to protect the then embryonic Shiite clerical regime.
Over the years, it has morphed into a vast economic and political empire. Rather than the elected president, the force answers directly to Iran's supreme leader.
The United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom, along with other countries, classify the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organization.

articles.title: Tundu Lissu: After escaping the death penalty, what does his guilty verdict mean for Tanzania's democracy?

paras.en: On November 6, Tundu Lissu, leader of Tanzania's main opposition Chadema party, was sentenced to four years in prison for incitement following heavy unrest during the October 2025 elections.
The same day, he was cleared of treason charges — which could have meant a death sentence if he had been found guilty.
Lissu commented that the judiciary had acted under pressure and rejected the verdict due to the fact that incitement was not among the charges brought against him at the start of his trial in 2025.
Chadema officials have now signaled an intention to appeal the court decision. The government has not issued a statement on his conviction yet.
Tanzania's most dramatic trial in decades

Few opposition figures have shaped modern Tanzanian politics as dramatically as Lissu. A lawyer by training and one of the country's most outspoken critics of the ruling party Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), Lissu has spent years challenging the political establishment.

Over the years, he has been repeatedly arrested and detained. In 2017, he survived an attempt on his life by unknown gunmen outside his residence in the capital Dodoma, sustaining multiple bullet wounds.

His trial in the run-up to the October 2025 general election continued to keep him and the opposition in the public eye following his arrest in April that same year in the southwestern town of Mbinga.
Prosecuters accused Lissu of encouraging the public to prevent the 2025 election from taking place and charged him with one count of treason.
As legal evidence, they cited social media posts he had made, in which he was seen to be calling on Tanzanians to boycott the vote over concerns about possible electoral malpractice.
In the end, the election went ahead without Chadema on October 29. It was marred by violence on an unprecedented in scale in Tanzania, with security forces even firing live ammunition at protesters.

Francis Ibrahim, an independent political analyst based in Dar es Salaam, told DW that "heads have to roll from the law enforcement side who overstretched their mandate, all the way to the people who financed, planned and organized [this crackdown]."
Following the election violence and a nationwide internet shutdown and curfew, incumbent President Samia Suluhu Hassan was named winner with 98% of the vote.
What does the verdict mean for democracy?
Ibrahim believes that the removal of the capital treason charge could be interpreted as a move towards rapprochment with voters.
"What I can tell you is that they are looking for a political deescalation that could solve the crisis," he explained, adding that Lissu might yet get to have a small say in politics after all.

"There has to be a process of [creating] a new constitution, and it needs everybody on the table," he said, adding that Lissu might therefore perhaps be released early in order to partake in discussions and negotiations.

But in late July, when President Suluhu Hassan met with representatives of more than a dozen political parties to discuss national reconciliation and constitutional reform, Chadema officials were explicitly not party to the consultations.
Public opinion meanwhile varies on Lissu's verdict, with many Tanzanians saying that the trial was politically motivated in their view.
Ruqaya Mohammed, the National Deputy Secretary of the oppsition ACT-Wazalendo party's youth wing, told DW, "we are getting into a darker space in our political arena."
"I think it's the right time now, as a nation, to have open dialogue on some reforms, on the legal perspective and electoral reforms. Maybe if we manage ... that, we can see a light," she added.
Most others, however, remain reluctant to go on record for fear of reprisal. A musician and human rights advocate was among few who agreed to speak to DW — on the strict condition of anonymity.

In his view, Tanzanians simply are not free to express themselves publicly. "You saw the terror atmosphere and climate of fear outside the court premises when Tundu's judgement was ... read. Such is the broader display of what Tanzania looks like," he told DW.

"Opposition politics has been suppressed for years, and [Lissu's] conviction is just a continuation of what has been happening. It's a miracle that he is still alive. To put him in jail from four years is far from the worst-case scenario."
This article has been adapted from an episode of DW's AfricaLink podcast.

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina must return to Bangladesh to face her sentence

paras.en: For families who lost relatives in Bangladesh’s July-August 2024 uprising, Sheikh Hasina’s presence in India is far more than just a question of political refuge. Some are caring for injured relatives, while others have been left devastated by their losses. Parents have rooms that are now empty. When the ousted prime minister speaks to Bangladeshis from India, the question arises: Why should those who paid the price for democracy have to watch the very person they hold responsible for their suffering continue to intervene in Bangladesh’s politics from abroad?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In February 2025, the UN Human Rights Office estimated that as many as 1,400 people may have been killed during the 2024 uprising, with thousands more injured. It identified systematic repression by the former government, the security forces and violent elements of the Awami League, and concluded that there was an official policy of violent suppression that warranted further investigation into potential crimes against humanity. These were international findings of fact, not a criminal verdict.

Subsequent domestic proceedings dealt with individual responsibility. In November 2025, Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity, including instigating and abetting the atrocities and ordering lethal force against protesters. It also held her responsible under the doctrine of superior command responsibility and sentenced her to death in absentia. She has called the trial politically motivated. Her denial in no way diminishes the victims’ right to justice. Bangladesh has requested her extradition from India, but she remains there.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Under Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, the government is attempting to repair a damaged economy and to re-establish a political culture that has been badly scarred by years of autocratic rule. Yet Hasina’s supporters abroad continue to promote the prospect of her political comeback on social media. Such messages fuel uncertainty about the future of Bangladesh’s democratic transition, particularly for families still waiting for justice.

The elected government and all political organisations committed to that transition have a responsibility to defend it. They should respond to any attempts to destabilise it with factual information and legal action, keeping victims at the heart of their policies. But Bangladesh cannot address these concerns alone while Hasina remains in India.

In an interview with Prothom Alo, C Christine Fair, a political scientist at Georgetown University, said that Hasina had been useful to India and that New Delhi would not hand her over. But India’s decision to shelter Hasina is one issue; allowing her to continue intervening in Bangladesh’s politics from Indian territory is another.

In January 2026, Bangladesh’s Foreign Ministry accused Hasina of inciting violence to disrupt the forthcoming elections after she addressed a public event in New Delhi. Fair questioned why New Delhi appeared unwilling to restrain Hasina when it had previously persuaded foreign political figures, including the Dalai Lama and Aung San Suu Kyi, to exercise restraint. She suggested that India’s domestic politics explained the difference. From Bangladesh’s perspective, this raises questions about how much weight New Delhi gives to its neighbour’s concerns when they conflict with its own political calculations.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Whatever political considerations shape New Delhi’s position, Bangladesh’s extradition request must be assessed on its legal merits. A person’s political status does not automatically prevent extradition. Article 6 of the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty specifically excludes murder, incitement to murder and a number of related offences from the political offence exception. Other grounds and safeguards for refusal remain applicable.

Through sustained diplomatic engagement, the government of Bangladesh should make clear that Dhaka wants constructive relations with India on the basis of sovereign equality and expects a serious response to its extradition request. It should also ask New Delhi to ensure that its territory is not used to incite violence in Bangladesh or threaten its people. Specific incidents should be documented, and peaceful political expression should be clearly distinguished from calls for violence.

If India is serious about resetting its relationship with Bangladesh, it has to respect the democratic mandate of that country and acknowledge the suffering of its people. Protecting a former dictator from accountability will only serve to increase mistrust. Sheikh Hasina must return to Bangladesh to answer in person for the killings and abuses committed under her government and to face any further lawful proceedings. Her return must deliver justice to the victims and help restore the rule of law that Bangladesh is so keen to re-establish.
